**Honors and Congratulatory Resolutions**

**To the population of the Municipality of Poções, State of Bahia, on the occasion of the 131st anniversary of its political-administrative emancipation:**

Jô Moraes (Bloc/PCdoB, MG) – Resolution congratulating the municipality on the occasion of the Day of the Vigilant. Appeal to the Commission on Constitution and Justice and Citizenship for the approval of Project of Law No. 6,113, of 2009, regarding the regulation of activities or operations considered dangerous.

Nazareno Fonteles (PT, PI) – Expectative for the House to vote in favor of Legislative Decree No. 2,841-A, of 2010, regarding the regulation of the Support Fund for Family Agriculture within the Common Market of the South – MERCOSUR.

Marçal Filho (PMDB, MS) – Agreement to establish, through the National Supplementary Health Agency, a deadline for the performance of medical examinations through health plans.

Eudes Xavier (PT, CE) – Holding of the "Overcoming Poverty in Brazil" seminar in Fortaleza, State of Ceará. Review of poverty throughout Brazilian history. Importance of policies and programs to combat poverty implemented in the country. Data from the IBGE population census, reflecting the number of citizens living in extreme poverty in Brazil. Relevance of the National Program for Strengthening Family Agriculture – PRONAF.

Cesar Colnago (PSDB, ES) – Installation of the Mixed Parliamentary Front in Defense of Solid Economy.

Jilmar Tatto (PT, SP – as Leader) – Approval of a significant number of formal jobs created in the country. Launch of PAC 2 and the second phase of the "My House, My Life" program by President Dilma Rousseff. Creation by the Federal Government of specific programs for the technical qualification of Brazilian workers. Launch of anti-poverty programs in the country. Social reach of the "Brazil Without Poverty" plan.

**President (Márcio Macedo) – Greetings to the children of the Santo Antônio Institute of Padua, in the Municipality of Itabirito, State of Minas Gerais, present in the gallery of this House.**

Assis Melo (Bloc/PCdoB, RS) – Commemoration of the 121st anniversary of the founding of Caxias do Sul Municipality, State of Rio Grande do Sul. Celebration of the Grape Festival in the municipality. Performance of the metal-mechanic pole in Caxias do Sul and the region. Announcement of a strike movement by metalworkers in Caxias do Sul and the region for a salary increase.

Sueli Vidigal (PDT, ES) – Installation of a new Emergency Care Unit – UPA in the Municipality of Serra, State of Espírito Santo.

# **Requests and Resolutions**

## **Request for Information**

**Nº 683/2011** – From Mr. Antonio Carlos Mendes

**Nº 2.245/2011** – From Mr. Laercio Oliveira – So-

**Request** to the Most Excellent Minister of Defense, Mr. Nelson Azevedo Jobim, for information regarding recent legislative measures by the governments of Paraguay and Bolivia that facilitate the registration of vehicles in irregular situations in those countries, many of which are products of crimes committed in Brazil. (In accordance with Article 117, Section 19 and Article 117, Section 3 of the Internal Regulation.)

**Nº 2.246/2011** – From Mr. Eudes Xavier

**Request**, in accordance with Article 117, Section 19 and Article 117, Section 3 of the Internal Regulation, for the House to register in its annals votes of congratulations, commending the production of the *VALE DO ACARAÚ NOTÍCIAS* newspaper (Edition II – MAY 2011 – 3rd Edition).

**Nº 684/2011** – From Mr. Antonio Carlos Mendes

**Request** for information from the Minister of Foreign Relations, Mr. Antonio de Aguiar Patriota, regarding recent legislative measures by the governments of Paraguay and Bolivia that facilitate the registration of vehicles in irregular situations in those countries, many of which are products of crimes committed in Brazil.

**Nº 2.247/2011** – From Mr. Eudes Xavier

**Request**, in accordance with Article 117, Section 19 and Article 117, Section 3 of the Internal Regulation, for the House to register in its annals votes of congratulations, commending the publication *TODOS CONTRA O Crack* (All Against Crack) in March-April 2011, Issue 60, in the *Valorização e Promoção da Produção Científica, Tecnológica e Cultural da Universidade Federal do Ceará* (Valorization and Promotion of Scientific, Technological, and Cultural Production of the Federal University of Ceará) magazine.

**Nº 685/2011** – From Mr. Antonio Carlos Mendes

**Request** for information from the Minister of Mines and Energy regarding the Abreu de Lima Refinery in Pernambuco, in response to the accompanying questions.

**Nº 686/2011** – From Mr. Antonio Carlos Mendes

**Request** for information from the Minister of Development, Industry, and Foreign Trade regarding the Abreu de Lima Refinery in Pernambuco, in response to the accompanying questions.

**Nº 2.237/2011** – From Mr. Luiz Alberto – Request for a special session to commemorate 58 years of Petrobras on October 3, 2011 (Tuesday).

**Nº 2.250/2011** – From Mr. Eudes Xavier

**Request**, in accordance with Article 117, Section 19 and Article 117, Section 3 of the Internal Regulation, for the House to register in its annals votes of congratulations, commending *CARIRI REVISTA*, *O MUNDO PARA O CARIRI* (The World for Cariri), and *CARIRI PARA O MUNDO* (Cariri for the World) in their 2011 Edition 1.

**Nº 2.238/2011** – From Ms. Luciana Santos – Request to include in the Order of Business Bill 6699/2002, which amends Article 40, Paragraph 9 of the Federal Constitution of 1988.

**REQUEST NO. 2241, 2011**

The most relevant agenda items of the 100th International Labour Conference, approved by majority votes in historic votes within the International Labour Organization (ILO) system, include:

1. **Convention and Recommendation on Domestic Workers**: Approved by 396 votes in favor, 16 against, and 63 abstentions. Undoubtedly, this was one of the most significant and memorable events of the 21st century in ILO history and the international trade union movement's struggle for social rights, equality of opportunity, sustainability of the system, and democratic governance, as it affects over 100 million domestic workers worldwide, with incalculable benefits for society.

2. **Recommendation to the 2012 Conference on Establishing Social Security Floors**: Approved by 431 votes in favor, 17 against, and 14 abstentions. During this debate, there was extensive discussion on social security floors. While all agreed on a minimum floor, some representatives from countries with more stable social protection systems expressed skepticism that governments and employers might use the floor to "level down."

3. **Election of the ILO Administration Council**: Our Secretary of International Relations, Nilton Souza (Neco), was elected with 105 votes in a 106-member electoral college to represent all workers and employees in Brazil and join other council members and council members from around the world. This was achieved through an unprecedented agreement between the Confederation of International Trade Unions and the National Federation of Chinese Trade Unions, resulting in a single workers' list, including a Chinese representative as a titular member of the Administration Council. This initiative gained support from most international trade unions, particularly the Trade Union Confederation. Neco stated that it is important to strengthen unity and workers' action to confront the crisis and the challenges of globalization.

Additionally, the budget for the ILO for the 2012-2013 period, a resolution on managing multilateral system policies and the ILO's role, and important decisions by the International Labour Standards Commission were all approved. The Commission included the inclusion of some countries and the removal of others from the list of the top 25 countries violating ILO norms, concerning workers' rights and freedom of association worldwide.

Finally, I would like to address another issue. At the request of Senator Paulo Paim from the PT of Rio Grande do Sul, the Permanent Subcommission on Employment and Social Security, which operates under the ILO system, held a meeting with railway workers. These workers, aged between 70 and 80, face losing their health plans due to financial instability. Before closing this fund, we are appealing to Ministers Carlos Lupi (Labor) and Alfredo Nascimento (Transportation) to address this issue.
32216   Thursday, June 23, 2011   DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES   June 2011

The Commission on Social Affairs of the Senate, through RONORTE, which will be the largest terminal of this railway, in my state, in Rondonópolis, one of the central and important cities for agribusiness, held a public hearing last Tuesday to discuss the topic: Decent work and the health of railway workers. Senator Paulo Paim proposed a series of debates focusing on various issues of interest to workers, such as the regulation of the profession, reduction of working hours and charges, collective bargaining and trade union freedom, workplace accidents, among others.

I sympathize with the situation. How can we ensure that approximately 13,000 railway workers, aged between 70 and 80, will lose their right to a health plan and remain without options? We need to consider the possibility of obtaining public funding to replenish the reserve fund and keep the Railway Workers' Health Plan (PLANSFER) operational.

The representative of the National Federation of Railway Workers, João Edacir Calegari Morais, reminded that a solution to the case should be adopted in less than 30 days to avoid the closure of the workers' plan. After listening to the representatives of the railway workers, Senator Paim announced that the Commission would provide full support to their claims and would request a meeting with Ministers of Labor, Carlos Lupi, and of Transport, Alfredo Nascimento, to discuss the matter. At this moment, I would like to reinforce the appeal to the Ministers to ensure that this federal funding for the railway workers' plan is done as soon as possible, as we cannot overlook the importance of the railway family.

Looking back, we can see that railway workers took immense pride in their profession. Indeed, there is a sense of profound respect for labor and an unparalleled spirit of camaraderie. One could say that this profession is in the DNA of this country's development, and we must honor these brave workers.

The Ministry of Transport, through Minister Alfredo Nascimento and General Director of DNIT, Luiz Antonio Pagot, has been carrying out structural and extremely important works in our state. I would like to highlight the duplication of the highway section between Rondonópolis and Posto Gil, passing through Cuiabá, and the urban section of Lourencinho to the Police Highway, already under construction. This week, we also obtained the environmental license for the duplication of the section from Posto Trevão to the future terminal of FER-GO. With these infrastructure works, Rondonópolis will be more accessible to tourists, who can also enjoy other attractions.

With a modern airport, whose expansion works were inaugurated last week. I have always worked on this project, concerned with meeting the logistical demands created by the region's development.

The Municipal Airport Maestro Marinho Franco was built with funds from the National Aerodromic Fund. More recently, I successfully secured Ministry of Tourism funds for expanding the passenger terminal, in partnership with the City Hall. With this, the airport gained space for the boarding lounge, access doors with metal detectors, restrooms, a baby changing station, a baggage claim area with a moving walkway, a commercial area, a snack bar, and an information desk. The project also includes duplicating the number of airline check-in counters and providing space for the Federal Police. The funds also ensured the modernization of flight safety equipment.

The goal is to make this airport a major hub for the one in Várzea Grande during peak passenger seasons, such as during the 2014 World Cup. To make this project a reality, I took a team from the Regional Air Command – COMAR to the city in 1997 for a meeting, where the need and possibility of building a new terminal were discussed.

With COMAR's approval, we began planning a new, larger, better-equipped structure on a plot of land not as close to homes as the then José Salmen Hanse Airport. At the time, Rondonópolis and the region received support from the Federal Government, which released funds through the Federal Airport Aid Program – PROFAA for the project.

Inaugurated in 2000, the new Maestro Marinho Franco Airport, equipped with night lighting, brought more tourists, business people, and hope for the treatment of patients who needed urgent transport. New opportunities arrived through the skies over Rondonópolis. The new structure attracted more passengers, who used the airport for daily flights to Cuiabá and other municipalities. The airport's operation was essential for the establishment of companies like Nortox and Petrópolis Brewery, as well as other ventures that boosted the local economy and created jobs for hundreds of families.

Over the years, as passenger traffic increased, the facility became outdated and needed improvements both in infrastructure and in acquiring necessary equipment, as required by the National Civil Aviation Agency – ANAC.

A partnership between the Diário do Nordeste newspaper and the Ari de Sá Cavalcanti School will provide Ceará's students with a valuable tool for performing well on the National High School Exam (ENEM) in 2011. Of the 16 fascicles, one is distributed each Friday, with the first issue reaching students on June 9th. This is the second consecutive year that the Diário do Nordeste has engaged in this segment, with approximately 230,000 registrations for the ENEM this year alone in Ceará.

As one of the most reputable schools in the state, Ari de Sá's teachers have crafted questions modeled after the ENEM format, covering all relevant areas. This year, in addition to 180 questions and an essay, a new feature is the inclusion of a foreign language, allowing students to choose between English and Spanish.

The newspaper and school's joint initiative includes virtual simulations and video lessons with Ari de Sá's teachers, one day after the printed material is published, to help students understand and clarify any doubts they may have. A comprehensive simulation will be held at the Universidade de Fortaleza (UNIFOR) at the end of the 16 fascicles.

Within the program, content on Essay and Language, Codes and their Technologies will be published on June 16th, 23rd, and 30th, and the first issue was released on June 9th. Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen legislators, after 44 days of strike, the teachers of the municipal network of Casa Nova, Bahia, ended the strike and returned to work on last Thursday, June 16th. Organized by the Union of Workers in Education of the State of Bahia (APLB), and with the broad support of several other civil society organizations, the teachers had been camping out on the grass in front of the city hall as a form of pressure on the local mayor to meet their demands.

The return to work was the result of an agreement signed between the APLB/Union and the city mayor, in which he committed to fulfilling the demands for better working conditions and school infrastructure.

It cannot be said that the strike was unjust. Just as it cannot be denied that the municipal administration, despite all the difficulties inherent to a small city located in the semi-arid region, has been making efforts to improve public education conditions.

Therefore, common sense prevailed, and teachers and the municipality reached an agreement that ended the strike, so that the student community would not be further harmed.

Those who know the reality of the semi-arid region understand the difficulties that teachers and students face on a daily basis. Despite the annual recovery work, there are physical deficiencies in the schools of Casa Nova, as well as a scarcity of teaching and learning materials. Often, the school lunch is not enough to meet the demand, especially considering that for many, this is the only meal of the day.

The same can be said about school transportation, which is carried out on rural roads that, during rainy seasons, become extremely difficult to navigate. In the case of Casa Nova, there is an additional aggravating factor: many students who live in the rural areas have to cross the São Francisco River by boat to reach the bus that takes them to school on the other side.

Thus, as we can see, these problems are complex, different from those faced in larger cities, but they must be addressed through an agreement between teachers and the municipality.

The agreement that ended the strike includes the national salary floor, the availability of 73 buses for student transportation within the municipality, which has one of the largest territorial extensions in Bahia, and the reorganization of five schools starting from the June/July recess period in 2011. By assuming these commitments, Mayor Orlando Nunes guaranteed that he will take the necessary measures to also resolve the school problem in the Entroncamento community and resume the salary and career plan for the category.

On the same June 25th, 1822, the city council of Cachoeira, a city of over 32,000 inhabitants, located on the Paraguaçu River and inscribed as a National Historical Heritage Site, declared its independence from Portugal. The people of Cachoeira had been at the forefront of the movement that led to the declaration of independence of Bahia, which occurred almost two months later, on October 2nd, 1822.

I am translating the provided text from Brazilian Portuguese to English, preserving the original context and meaning:

We celebrate the first concrete act of our independence, remembering that in the State of Rio de Janeiro, despite being a pioneer in Brazil, it was not until one year later, on July 2, 1823, that it consolidated in Bahia. That's why the date is considered a milestone for Bahians. To reach this day, free and sovereign, Brazilians and Bahians in particular have had to fight many battles. But the struggle of Bahians for freedom had the effective participation of indigenous peoples, identified symbolically as the true Brazilians, the owners of the land, and the mixed-race populations with still-enslaved blacks, who combined their efforts with other combatants. That's why, in the commemorations of July 2, in addition to civic and military rituals, we honor the figures of the Indians and the caboclo (a term for indigenous-descended Brazilians) and cabocla (female caboclo).

We know, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, that the process of a people's independence is not solidified solely through decrees. One hundred and eighty-eight years later, Bahia consolidated its independence with a democratic government elected to serve the interests of the population. This is in contrast to the rest of the country, where we have lived the last 40 years, until the victory of democratic forces represented by Governor Jacques Wagner and his entire support base, under the tyranny of oligarchies that insisted on keeping Bahia in backwardness regarding freedom of expression and free manifestation of its people.

But just as the Bahians of 1823 said no to tyranny and elected a democratic government, the Bahians of today also participate in this democratic government that they themselves chose. They consolidate independence in the manifestations of social movements, such as blacks, landless people, indigenous peoples, African-derived religious communities, and the LGBT population. They say no to any process of tyranny that threatens to take away their hard-won freedom.

That's why I want to not only congratulate the Bahian people on this date, but also the people of Cachoeira, for their invaluable contribution to our independence. I also commend Governor Jacques Wagner, who, with the gesture of transferring the government seat to the city of Cachoeira, honors a people that has fought so hard for full democracy today.

Ladies and Gentlemen, I take this opportunity to request that my speech be included in this House's record.

Mr. President, I also request that we acknowledge the hundreds of deaths on Brazilian roads, which unfortunately occur every year. It is essential that the National Program to Combat Road Traffic Deaths comes to the forefront to reduce these numbers.

Sir, Madam and Gentlemen Deputies, even though regional disparities remain stark, Brazil became less unequal last decade, thanks to Bolsa Família, according to data released by the IBGE demographic census in the Folha de S.Paulo newspaper on Sunday, June 19. The report delved into how the movement affected cities throughout northeastern Brazil.

Northeastern cities led the gains in per capita income, with Paulista cities lagging behind. Among the 50 municipalities with over 100,000 inhabitants that experienced the most progress between 2000 and 2010, half are in the Northeast, and only one is in São Paulo. The newspaper states that, according to experts, the rise in the minimum wage and Bolsa Família help explain the reduction in disparities over the past decade.

From 2000 to 2010, average income rose 3% in Paulista cities and 46% in Maranhão cities.

Note that disparities persist, despite this.

In the past 14 years, 73% of Brazilian families have changed social classes due to increased income, a total of 143 million people.

This mobility is superior to that seen in the United States, Sweden, or Canada over such a short period. Data from a survey by the IPC Maps consultancy.

In the list of the 50 cities that advanced the least, 36 are in São Paulo. Correcting values from 2000 for inflation over 10 years by the INPC (IBGE indicator), 12 even experienced a slight decline in average income. Nine of these are Paulista cities.

It is natural for poorer municipalities to have more room for advancement. However, this is not always the case in a country accustomed to inequality. For example, in the 1980s, São Paulo's average household income rose 17%, while Maranhão's increased by only 7%.

Mr. Eduardo Sciarra (DEM-PR) – Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, I request that my statement be recorded in which I express our disappointment at the fact that, in the week past, the Federal Government announced the Safra Plan for 2011/2012, but made no mention of the Disaster Fund. This House, the National Congress as a whole, has over the years approved all the necessary regulation for the implementation of this fund, which will mitigate the suffering of rural producers who work outdoors in a high-risk activity. We broke the monopoly of reinsurance in Brazil to achieve this. However, unfortunately, the regulation has still not been put in place, and the decree that was supposed to resolve this situation will not cover this harvest.

The law establishing the Fund was sanctioned by the President of the Republic last August with the promise of applying 4 billion reais through public bonds. Yet, almost a year later, the Government has not regulated it, which, in practice, renders all the efforts of Congress in discussing this important legal instrument ineffective.

Worse, rural producers will once again face a harvest assuming all the risks inherent to their activity. I am well acquainted with the dilemmas of Brazilian rural producers. A rural property is a business exposed to rains, droughts, and all sorts of weather conditions. The regulation of the law will bring more security to farmers during adverse climatic events. Therefore, this delay is unacceptable, considering that the Legislative branch has been working for years to overcome a series of difficulties, and rural producers are disappointed with this decision as they expected the protection of the Fund for this year's harvest.

It is worth noting that this sector accounts for a significant portion of the national PIB, but it is the only one to bear all the risks inherent to its activities. I believe it is the Government's responsibility to create support mechanisms for agriculture, such as the Disaster Fund.

The main objective of the Disaster Fund is to make agricultural insurance viable through the creation of a private consortium made up of insurance companies and re-insurers, which would be subsidized by the Federal Government. The consortium would be responsible for managing and covering the risks. Here at the National Congress, year after year, month after month, day after day, we fight for social policies to take regional disparities into account. We are proud to see that the results of this hard battle are already being felt.

Ms. and Mr. Deputies, we see with a certain naturalness, but not without a certain pride, that the results of these struggles are already being observed. An example is found in the press. The São Paulo newspaper Folha de S.Paulo published, last Sunday, June 19, a report titled "Inequality declines between Northeast and SP." In the article, experts state that Brazil became less unequal in the last 10 years. Among the reasons for this decrease in inequality, as analysts point out, are the increase in the minimum wage and social programs such as Bolsa Família.

The report highlights, based on data from the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE), that the Northeast region grew more than other regions. And, in particular, some states had higher income gains. Sergipe State recorded a 41% growth. Aracaju, the capital of Sergipe, was the Northeastern capital with the highest growth.

Since 1995, Sergipe State has recorded growth rates above the Brazilian and world averages. While, in the period from 2004 to 2005, Brazil grew by 3.2%, the Northeast region had a 4.6% growth rate. In the same period, the world average was 4.8%. Well, Mr. President, Ms. and Mr. Deputies, in this time frame, Sergipe State's growth reached 5.5%. In other words, above the world, Brazilian, and Northeastern averages.

Another proof that Sergipe has been greatly benefited by the current policies can be found in the analysis of the National Household Sample Survey (PNAD), released last month, on June 12. According to this survey, Sergipe recorded the highest average household income and the highest per capita income in the Northeast. These numbers, Mr. President, Ms. and Mr. Deputies, fill me and my fellow citizens with pride.

But these numbers are not mere coincidence. The state government has been working to improve the quality of life for Sergipanos. The policy of regionalizing Sergipe, which prioritizes the interiorization of industries, creating jobs throughout the state, and opening up opportunities for all.

These efforts have resulted in Sergipe having the highest average household income and per capita income in the Northeast. These figures, Mr. President, Ms. and Mr. Deputies, fill me and my fellow citizens with pride.

However, these numbers are not enough. We must continue to work to ensure that all Sergipanos have access to quality health services, education, and infrastructure. We must strive for a more equitable and prosperous future for our state.

But these numbers also underscore the urgent need for the regulation of Constitutional Amendment 29. As the PNAD shows, while Sergipe has made significant progress, there is still much work to be done. We must ensure that all states allocate the necessary resources for health, education, and social programs.

It is unconscionable that some states fail to allocate adequate resources for health care. As we strengthen primary care, we automatically strengthen the reduction of investments in tertiary and secondary care.

Therefore, we urge the House to prioritize the regulation of Constitutional Amendment 29 this semester.

Mr. MENDONÇA FILHO (DEM-PE, Leader) – Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Parliamentarians, I stand in this House this morning to speak on matters of interest to Brazil.

I begin by commenting on an international incident that unfortunately affects our country, on which, in my view, the Brazilian Government, which should adopt a firmer, clearer, and more effective position, has been silent. I am referring specifically to the decision of Bolivian President Evo Morales, through a presidential decree, to legalize cars circulating in that country, most of which were stolen from countries that make up the MERCOSUR – Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay, and primarily Brazil – and Chile.

This measure taken by President Morales and recently publicized is, in my opinion, absurd and mistaken. It has outraged a significant portion of the Brazilian population because, on the one hand, it will create a certain market for the sale of stolen vehicles within our territory; and on the other, it will impose an additional financial burden on Brazilian society.

Everyone knows that the cost of insurance in Brazil is determined, among other factors, by risk. Therefore, theft is undoubtedly the factor that most increases the cost of insuring a vehicle in our territory.

I therefore leave this record. We are submitting a request, which will likely be considered next week, starting with President Marco Maia's speech, to present a motion of repudiation and make our position known regarding this mistaken decision adopted by the Bolivian Government, through President Evo Morales.

I would like to make two brief notes. First, tomorrow, June 23rd, the Mariano Procópio Museum—the first museum in Brazil—will celebrate its 90th anniversary. This date holds significant importance for us Minas Gerais residents, especially for me, as a resident of Juiz de Fora, as it coincides with the 190th anniversary of the opening of the first paved road connecting Rio de Janeiro, Petrópolis, and Juiz de Fora, the União Indústria Road.

Recently, on Saturday, President Fernando Henrique, in an interview with O Globo newspaper, when asked about what has changed in 80 years, noted that when he was born, 80 years ago, the only paved road was the União Indústria Road. This is a remarkable feat, all thanks to the pioneering spirits of Bernardo Mascarenhas, Henrique Halfeld, and Mariano Procópio, a close friend of Emperor Dom Pedro II, who spent their summer vacations where there is now a beautiful park and a lovely house, which has since become the Mariano Procópio Museum. It is the second collection from the Imperial period, boasting a stunning photo collection, many taken by Dom Pedro II himself, and paintings—a wonderful collection.

Therefore, I would like to mark the 90th anniversary of the Mariano Procópio Museum and request that the House communicate this to the museum's board. I also request support from the House to intervene with the Ministry of Culture, as unfortunately, the first museum created in Brazil is currently closed to the public due to a lack of funding for the necessary renovations.

My second note is regarding an article titled "Industrial Policy, BNDES, and Budgetary Priorities" about Measure Provisional (MP) No. 526, which makes a significant transfer of income. On Wednesday, June 8th, at 9 PM, the Chamber of Deputies rejected a motion of reproach regarding President Dilma not having received the Iranian lawyer and Nobel Peace Prize winner Shirin Ebadi in 2003. Shortly after, we voted on MP No. 526.

The National Congress must remain vigilant. This is a brutal transfer of income of 55 billion reais to cover the difference between the government's interest rate on borrowings (Selic at 12.25%) and the interest rates on loans from the Industrial Policy Support Program (PSI at around 5% to 8%). As Milton Friedman once said, "There is no free lunch," and as public finance managers affirm, "Money does not have a stamp." With these 55 billion reais authorized, we will reach an astronomical figure.

Without review by the speaker) – Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen of the House, I would like to highlight, at this moment, Legislative Project No. 2,841-A of 2010, from the Brazilian Parliamentary Representation of the MERCOSUR, which is on the agenda for today – I do not know if we will have a quorum to vote on it. We have followed with great interest this project that deals with food and nutritional security and the human right to food, provided by the strengthening of family farming – in this case, the creation of the MERCOSUL Family Farming Support Fund. We had the opportunity, in the Commission on Constitution, Justice, and Citizenship, to cast a favorable vote for its advancement to the plenary session of this House.

It is important to demonstrate the role of Brazil and the weight of its financial contribution to this Fund, which is 70%, while Argentina's is 27%, Paraguay's is 1%, and Uruguay's is 2%. Although, mind you, the resources are still limited, this has symbolic value: the integration of South America in favor of small family farmers. At the same time, this vision of international solidarity partnership, based on the spirit of equity and social justice, is reflected in the fact that as the largest and richest nation of the MERCOSUR, Brazil must make a proportionally greater contribution.

From this historical and social perspective, pauperization becomes evident throughout Brazil's historical trajectory in the context of extreme disparities.

One of the milestones in Brazil's recent history of defending social rights is observed through the democratic experiences lived in the 1980s. Starting from a still repressive scenario, given the military dictatorship period, collective resistance movements emerge against the culture of fear and obedience to uniforms.

The emergence of new social movements in Brazil from the 1980s, such as urban social movements (e.g., CEBs - Church Base Communities), the strengthening of new urban and rural sindicalism, the feminist movement, the ecological movement, among others, contributed to the consolidation of new democratic experiences in the political arena.

According to Vera Teles (2006), in the 1930s, the labor contract served as a certificate of civic belonging. The law, instead of guaranteeing and universalizing rights, stripped individuals of their citizenship prerogatives and created a fracture between the figure of the worker and that of the uncivil poor. The corporate social protection system, of state nature, was geared towards workers integrated into the labor market. Those involved in the productive sector, unable to work due to some life vicissitude, such as illness or disability, were left out.

The effects of the debt crisis were profound: widespread poverty in Latin America, a crisis in public social services, unemployment, an increase in informal work, and a shift in production towards export-oriented industries at the expense of internal needs.

Facing the possibility of financial collapse, neoliberal discourse suited Brazilian society, especially in the 1990s. Adjustments in fiscal policy, coupled with cuts in social spending and public policies, aimed to stabilize the economy. This period witnessed a reevaluation of 1988's achievements, with reforms announced under the Collor and FHC governments dismantling the Brazilian state, opening the country to the market, particularly to financial speculators.

According to the authors, the privatization process in Brazil transferred a significant portion of public assets to foreign capital. As a result, there was no obligation for privatized companies to purchase inputs from Brazil, leading to the decline of a portion of the national industrial park and a significant loss of jobs.

The 1988 Constitution expanded social rights and the field of social protection under state responsibility, with significant impacts on policy design, the definition of users and benefits. According to Luciana Jaccoud (2009), especially from the 1990s to 2010, the Brazilian state began operating with a broader range of social policies, addressing social problems that emerged on the public agenda.

Examples include: the Food and Nutrition Security Policy; the Eradication of Child Labor Program; the Bolsa Família Program; the institutionalization of the National Social Assistance Policy, approved at the IV Social Assistance Conference in December 2003 in Brasília; and the consolidation of the Basic Norm that implements the Single System of Social Assistance (NOB/SUAS/2005), by the National Council of Social Assistance. These public policies and programs have significant impacts on the lives of the poorest and most vulnerable segments, who are socially unprotected.

During the Lula government, the implementation of the Bolsa Família Program unified various existing income transfer programs in Brazil, such as Bolsa Escola, Bolsa Alimentação, Vale Gás, and Cartão Alimentação. This program is characterized by direct income transfers with conditions, benefiting families in poverty and extreme poverty.

The program integrates the Zero Hunger Program, which aims to ensure the human right to adequate food, promoting food security and contributing to the achievement of citizenship by the most vulnerable population to hunger.

Bolsa Família is structured around three main axes: income transfer, conditions, and complementary programs. Income transfer provides immediate relief from poverty. Conditions reinforce access to basic social rights in education, health, and social assistance areas. Complementary programs aim to empower families so that beneficiaries can overcome their vulnerability.

According to Marcio Pochmann (2010), based on IBGE data, between 2003 and 2008, the average family income in the lowest 10% grew by 9.1% annually, while the average per capita income of the highest 10% grew by 1.6%. This is attributed to the policy of increasing the real minimum wage, which injected R$1 trillion into the earnings of low-wage workers over this period.

The Bolsa Família Program, among others, is supported by the Social Assistance Program, particularly the Continuous Benefit (BPC) program. It has resulted in a significant increase in income transfers to the most vulnerable segments of the population.
June 2011                     CHAMBER OF DEPUTIES DAILY JOURNAL                         Thursday 23   32243

The Brazilian population's extreme poverty, as indicated by the 2010 IBGE census data, reveals a concerning reality: 16.27 million Brazilians, or 8.5% of the total population, live in extreme poverty. A significant 59% of this population is concentrated in the Northeast Region, with 9.6 million people affected.

This poverty is not uniform; 53.3% of those in extreme poverty reside in urban areas, 50.9% are under 19 years old, and 39.9% are aged 14 or younger. Gender plays a role, with 50.5% being women and 49.5% men. Furthermore, 70.8% of the extremely poor are black (pardo and preto), and 26% are illiterate, with 15 years or more of education.

The data highlights the multifaceted nature of Brazilian poverty, including urban and rural poverty, with characteristics that deepen social class asymmetries, such as generational, gender, and racial/ethnic markers. This complexity necessitates a nuanced approach when discussing poverty reduction strategies.

Sônia Rocha (2005) emphasizes that the discussion around poverty lines should not solely focus on income indicators but also consider the determination of poverty lines. Studies on poverty lines establish a monetary value that intersects with the expenditure required to meet the basic needs of an individual, based on the total population's parameters, divided into two subgroups: those below the poverty line and those below the indigence line.

Rocha (2005) further explains that those considered poor are individuals unable to meet the minimum needs of society. Indigents, a subset of the poor, have even lower incomes, barely sufficient for nutritional needs. The indigence line aligns with food expenditure, while the poverty line relates to a broader set of vital needs beyond food, such as clothing.

Amartya Sen (2000), an Indian economist, suggests that poverty identification should consider both low income and the deprivation of capabilities. He highlights that various factors, including age, gender roles and social responsibilities, epidemiological conditions, and location, should be taken into account when designing public policies aimed at reducing inequality and poverty.

This comprehensive approach to understanding poverty has influenced international organizations' perspectives on the subject, as reflected in World Bank reports from 2000 to 2001, which differ from reports from 1990. In the 1990 report, poverty was primarily defined as the inability to meet basic needs, whereas later reports incorporated a broader understanding of poverty.

According to the World Bank's reports from 2000 and 2001, poverty is analyzed as a multifaceted phenomenon resulting from multiple deprivations caused by economic, political, and social processes that interact with each other. Based on Amartya Sen's theories, the World Bank's Human Development Program (PNUD) defines human development as a process aimed at expanding individual freedoms.

Pierre Salama and Blanche Destremau (1999) highlight that the PNUD's elaborations, drawing upon Amartya Sen's work, consider poverty not only as an economic category marked by income insufficiency and material scarcity, but also as a political and social category reflecting the lack of rights, opportunities, and hope.

The PNUD views human development as a process that seeks to enhance the possibilities offered to individuals. These possibilities are infinite and evolve over time, encompassing aspects such as: the chance to lead a long and healthy life, the acquisition of knowledge, and access to necessary resources for a decent standard of living.

According to the PNUD, poverty signifies the absence of the essentials for well-being, representing a denial of opportunities and choices fundamental for human development. It stems from individual incapacities, particularly in securing survival within the labor market.

The role of the state, as perceived by these international organizations, is to remove individuals from this condition of incapacity by integrating them into the labor market and reinforcing their human capabilities.

Critically, these concepts of poverty focus on individual incapacities, implying that the poor are those unable to ensure their survival, especially within the labor market. This perspective raises questions about the structure of the state, particularly in the context of Brazil's historical narrative, where a sense of citizenship remains challenging to attain.

Consequently, the notion of poverty should be carefully considered, taking into account the socio-political characteristics of each country. The state's fundamental role is to guarantee policies that ensure immediate income for those entirely devoid of survival conditions, such as the poor and marginalized.

In this regard, initiatives implemented under the Lula government, such as raising the minimum wage, expanding popular credit, and supporting civil society initiatives for job creation and income generation, like the Solid Economy, have been crucial in reducing poverty and social inequalities in Brazil.

Regarding popular credit policies, the focus is on rural credit programs, primarily aimed at family farming. The National Program for Family Farming Strengthening (PRONAF) finances individual or collective projects that generate income for farmers.

Family farmers and landless settlers benefit from various government programs in Brazil, aimed at alleviating poverty and promoting sustainable development in rural areas. The National Rural Credit Program (PRONAF) offers specific lines of credit with low-interest rates and favorable terms, catering to the unique needs of different target groups.

The PRONAF Semi-Arid Line specifically finances projects focused on living with the semi-arid regions, promoting sustainable agroecosystems, and improving infrastructure, including water access. The program also supports women and young farmers through dedicated credit lines.

The Purchase and Sale of Food (PAA) program, established in 2003 as part of the Zero Hunger Program, facilitates the direct acquisition of food at market-fair prices, benefiting family farmers and rural communities.

Another significant initiative is the Territories of Citizenship Program, which aims to overcome poverty and generate employment and income in rural areas through sustainable territorial development. This program involves a collaboration between the Federal Government, states, and municipalities.

According to data from the Ministry of Agriculture (MDA), between 2003 and 2009, the PAA purchases totaled R$2.5 billion, benefiting 635,500 family farmer households and, on average, 7.7 million people annually through food donations.

Mr. Artur Bruno (PT-CE, without revision) - Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, a lot has been discussed in recent days about the differentiated contracting regime. Last week, we approved this provisional measure.

Next week, we will discuss the highlights made to the matter to conclude this debate and this deliberation here at the Chamber. After that, it will go to the Senate.

Unfortunately, the population is quite misinformed about this provisional measure. There is a strategy, often used in the Nazi regime, which consists of repeating a lie until it seems true, by those who want to pass as truth what is not, in the sense that the Dilma Government is trying to keep secret the works for the Cup and the Olympics that will be achieved with this differentiated contracting regime.

First of all, there is no secrecy! It's a differentiated process that several countries already adopt for this contracting regime, where contractors receive from the Government the specifications of a work, that is, what needs to be done. According to these specifications, they present their proposals. Then, the Government, obviously, presents everything transparently to the Union Court of Accounts and the Union General Control. Therefore, there is no secrecy.

When there is competition and a company becomes the winner, the Government will publish everything so that society knows, transparently, what happened in that competition process. What is being tried with this differentiated contracting regime is to avoid the overcharging that is common in public works, at the municipal, state, or even federal levels. We want to make savings for the public coffers and promote agility in these processes.

We know that the 2014 World Cup is approaching, we will have the 2013 Confederations Cup, clearly, the time is short, urgent, and we need to ensure agility, promptness in the works, and better prices for the public coffers.

Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, interviews with the Governor of Sergipe, Marcelo Déda, were published yesterday in Valor Econômico and today in Estado, in which he expresses his opinions on tax reform and the pre-salt.

Déda stated that tax reform cannot be limited to the unification of ICMS among the Northeast, North, and Central-West States. Tax reform must ensure revenue that instruments a policy of regional development, so necessary for these regions.

I believe this is a good opportunity for Parliament to reflect on a fundamental topic for the Country, and instead of dividing us, it should unite us.

The fiscal war among the States weakens federal relations and must be overcome. The Lula Government reduced income inequality in Brazil, as never seen before, so we must think of a tax policy that perpetuates this achievement and does not deepen economic inequality among the States. The President herself, Dilma, stated in her inauguration speech: “Only tax reform allows for sustainable industrial expansion and growth.”

We need to reflect on the tax reform we want. Or better yet, if we want a real reform or just a new regulation of ICMS. A reform demands an agenda of negotiations that does not only have a technical focus, but also considers regional realities and the notion of the Country’s development as a whole, where it does not make sense to single out winners and losers.

Similarly, Déda pondered on the issue of the pre-salt. Agreeing that producing States have a right to receive a larger share of royalties, the Governor, however, advocated for a new distribution model, since this wealth belongs to the Country and should serve it entirely.

I have no doubt that the President has worked hard to ensure that the Northeast, North, and Central-West have their benefits secured and continue on the path of sustainable development and regional development to definitively overcome differences between the South, Southeast, Northeast, North, and Central-West of Brazil.

Today, I address this House to discuss an article published in the column of journalist Rubens Nóbrega in the Jornal da Paraíba of yesterday, June 21, 2011, addressing a matter of grave importance currently occurring in the state of Paraíba.

Governor Ricardo Coutinho, in defense of interests that do not belong to the people of Paraíba, is proposing a swap of a plot in Mangabeira, where the Academy of Police is located, for another in Geisel, where nothing currently functions.

The column of Rubens Nóbrega, broadcasted in the Jornal da Paraíba on June 21, 2011, states:

"Cuiá II

The deal may be good for the state, but in the way it is being handled, what Governor Ricardo Coutinho should call 'republican' I call the New Cuiá. I refer to the exchange of a plot in Mangabeira, where the Police Academy is located, for another in Geisel, where nothing currently functions.

His Excellency should call the deal 'republican' because, as he said yesterday on his radio program, the transaction is 'fair and just,' although the Mangabeira plot is twice as large and ten times as valuable as the Geisel plot. According to assessments, the Mangabeira plot is worth R$ 135.9 million, while the Geisel plot is valued at R$ 13.5 million. The difference is R$ 122.4 million.

In this case, it is indeed good for the state. Because neither the headquarters of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) nor the Scotland Yard of Britain, together, would be worth R$ 122.4 million.

This new complex or security public center must be something from another world, then. It must be something from a planet called Sunflower, which orbits a sun called Ricardo Coutinho.

If the explanations given yesterday by the astro-king and the figures provided by the incomparable Clilson Júnior, the entrepreneur who will secure this little corner, hold true, he will invest in Geisel an amount that would allow him to build, among other things:

- A shopping center the size of the Manaíra Shopping or, ambitiously, the size of the one that entrepreneur Roberto Santiago plans to build in Mangabeira, on what would be – exactly – the site of the Police Academy;

- Six emergency and trauma hospitals, each 22,500 square meters, roughly the size of the HT that is ready to operate in Campina Grande, but will only do so when the people forget that it was completed during the previous government;

- Two emergency and trauma hospitals with the same dimensions as the Campina Grande HT, fully equipped;

- Fifteen integral schools with capacity for 400 students each, similar to those recently inaugurated by the City Hall of the Capital in Bessa, with two floors, ten classrooms, computer and science labs, arts room, video room, library, bathrooms, administration, directorate, teachers' room, and a secretariat, plus a gymnasium."

In the Federal Chamber, only 8.7% of parliamentarians are women. On average, there is a 9% female representation across all spheres of the Brazilian legislative power. This is lower than the participation of women in Arab countries.

Some say that burqas do not exist in Brazil, and I say they do, the invisible burqas. Others claim there is no guillotine, but there is. The guillotine that decapitated feminist women during the French Revolution still exists in Brazil in an invisible form. We are in the unenviable position of being the second-to-last country in the Americas—above only Haiti and Belize—in terms of female representation in Parliament.

Therefore, yesterday we officially launched a manifesto from women in this House demanding gender alternation. For every man elected, a woman should be elected so that we can truly build democracy.

This is a fundamentally structuring discussion because the more women participate in lawmaking, budget preparation, public policy oversight, and other areas of power, the more we deconstruct the subalternity that exists in this country with regard to women.

With interest rates of 5.5% per annum, lower than the 6.75% fixed for most agricultural credit lines, the National Rural Support Program (PRONAMP) will have 48.2% more resources than stipulated for the 2010/2011 crop cycle. In this cycle, PRONAMP will make R$8.3 billion available to producers for investment and operating credit, with interest rates of 6.25% and repayment terms of up to 8 years for investment operations.

The annual gross income limit for eligibility in the program has also been increased from R$500,000 to R$700,000. Furthermore, the operational and beneficiary investment limits have been raised to R$400,000 and R$300,000, respectively.

The cooperative credit limit for the Aggregation of Value to Agricultural Production (PRODECOOP) program has also been increased, from R$50 million to R$60 million. This program finances up to R$2 billion at an interest rate of 6.75% per annum.

Producers will also have access to larger financing through the Modernization of Agriculture and Natural Resource Conservation Program (MODEAGRO), with the maximum amount per producer rising from R$300,000 to R$600,000, and collective credit increasing from R$900,000 to R$1.2 million. The repayment period has also been extended from 8 to 10 years.

In addition to financing warehouse construction and crop storage, the Irrigation and Storage Modernization Program (MODERINFRA) resources can also be used for input warehouses, storage facilities for harvesters, tractors, and other agricultural machinery.

The Agricultural and Livestock Plan is of extreme importance to the Brazilian agronomy sector, as it sets prices, proposes investment programs, and introduces changes to facilitate credit operations and producer access to resources. The good numbers in Brazilian agriculture are not only due to increased production areas but primarily the use of technology.

Although Russia is not part of the Euro-Judiciary and Public Ministry Union, I felt it was my right and even my duty to attend the hearing on its proposals, which have been before this House since 2009. Today, in the morning, I went there, accompanied by Deputy Michelletto, to address the issue of Brazilian meat imports, particularly from the states of Mato Grosso, Paraná, and Rio Grande do Sul.

While I am not directly representing my home state, I am here on behalf of the Parliamentary Group, representing all of Brazil and the interests of all Brazilian productive sectors.

We have received positive news, as efforts are being made to overcome the issues and for the Brazilian government to meet the requirements for importing Brazilian meat.

Vice President Michel Temer recently visited Russia and, upon his return to Brazil, sent a letter to the Russian government. Now, we are asking the ambassador and the Russian government to allow, as soon as possible, a Brazilian mission, with Brazilian technicians, to go to Russia to confirm that both the pork and chicken meat meet phytosanitary requirements.

Thank you, President, and a big hug to everyone.

The next speaker, Deputy Policarpo from the PT party, is the last due to our time constraints.

Yesterday, the servants of this House organized a beautiful mobilization in the corridors, requesting the support of Parliamentarians for the approval of career plans for the Judiciary and Public Ministry.

Yesterday, even with a low quorum, over 50 Parliamentarians signed the manifesto in support of the Bills No. 6,613 and No. 6,697. I request the transcription of this document.

The servants of the Judiciary in Brasília have been on strike since May 18th, for over a month. They are fighting for this House to approve the proposals and for the Judiciary to negotiate with the Executive.

Last Friday, there was a meeting, according to the STF, with Minister Cezar Peluso, President of the Supreme Federal Court, and Minister Miriam Belchior, Planning Minister.

We hope these negotiations will advance so that we can also do justice to the servants of the Judiciary and Public Ministry.

Thank you, President.

I present to this House a matter of utmost importance to the people of our country: actions to combat chemical dependency and attention to users of illicit drugs.

This maneuver, stemming from Provisional Measure 527, undermines oversight bodies such as the Court of Auditors, the right to review government-estimated budgets before selecting responsible companies for executing projects. The action goes against constitutional principles.

Ladies and gentlemen, once budgets for these projects are kept entirely secret, values can be negotiated at inflated prices, as contractors will ultimately set the final cost, and since the initial values are kept secret, they won't need to justify any potential overspending. We will create an environment where favored contractors are free from any conduct rules and have access to sensitive data.

A utopian world will be envisioned if we fail to recognize a significant gap in promoting the dark side of corruption. Millions of reais will flow through sports events, and this must be rigorously monitored by the Ministry of Public Works. It is well-known that even with the strictness of the Law of Tenders, some 2014 World Cup projects are already budgeted at astronomical figures, causing astonishment and losses for Brazilians.

I advocate and assure this House of the public disclosure of spreadsheets and full access for oversight entities, as World Cup and Olympic projects follow the same characteristics and procedures of other public works. I hope the Senate makes the necessary changes to Provisional Measure 527, altering the original text, excluding Section 3 of Article 6, which deals with secrecy, and promoting transparency, the primordial attribute of the Law of Tenders.

I hope, as do all Brazilians, that these sporting events generate employment, income, and investments in the country, and not an easy and illicit way for swindlers to make money at the people's expense.

Thank you, Mr. President.

A portion of taxpayers have been exercising their citizenship by taking actions to address the complexity of this issue, allocating a portion of their taxes to various funds aimed at expanding resources for social policies. I am certain that, in this struggle, it is of utmost importance that, in addition to formulating public policies, there is political will to increase the resources allocated to these actions.

The proposal also provides for an extension of the deadline to benefit both legal entities and natural persons, with the objective of allowing taxpayers to decide, during their annual adjustment, the exact amount they wish to allocate to drug policy funds.

Unfortunately, the current legislation discourages many taxpayers from making donations. This is due to the fact that the incentive is a percentage of the tax due, and until this number is determined, taxpayers are subject to a series of uncertainties regarding the deductible amount. This bureaucracy often becomes an obstacle to the significant influx of resources for implementing drug control policies.

Another provision of the bill requires that information about donations be provided annually by the responsible bodies for administering the accounts of the National, State, District, and Municipal Drug Policy Funds to the Federal Revenue Secretariat.

I have actively participated in this House's discussions on the drug issue, and I am a member of the Parliamentary Fronts to Combat Crack and Defend Community Therapies, as well as the Special Commission on Public Policies to Combat Drugs.

Like several other Parliamentarians, I have chosen this theme as one of the priorities of my mandate because I believe that Brazil needs to urgently address the drug problem by taking comprehensive and consistent measures in three fronts: prevention, treatment, and social reintegration of chemical dependents, as well as combating drug trafficking.

We are making progress in the debate on solutions in these three areas and want to offer the country a solid contribution to improve our legislation and public policies to combat drugs.

The Federal Government has also demonstrated that combating drugs is a priority, with some important measures already being taken.

We have noticed across Brazil that several states and municipalities are beginning to mobilize around this issue.

32290   Thursday, June 23, 2011   DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES   June 2011

I would like to express my solidarity with the family of José Góes dos Santos, and with all workers in collective transportation in Belo Horizonte. This week, a serious incident occurred in my city, Belo Horizonte, which has caused great sadness.

The assassination of José Góes dos Santos, a bus driver, while he was operating route 640 in the Jardim Leblon neighborhood, was a senseless act. Two individuals, fleeing from the police, boarded the bus and demanded that the driver stop at a location other than the designated stop point by the transportation company and the city's Traffic Department. The driver refused, fearing the potential consequences, including fines and job loss, as the buses are monitored. This was enough to prompt the individuals to shoot him.

This morning, as a result of the stoppage of activities, there has been genuine chaos in Venda Nova, particularly at the BHbus station in the region, which serves 60,000 passengers daily. Venda Nova is one of two districts of Belo Horizonte, the other being Barreiro, but like Barreiro, it has become integrated into the city and has an estimated population of over 300 people. There is not a single day that we are not confronted with a scene, a news report, or an image of extreme violence decimating workers, students, families, and shattering social bonds.

In Venda Nova, the murder of José Góes dos Santos while driving a bus was over a trivial matter. Two individuals on the run from the police boarded the bus and demanded that the driver stop at a location not designated by the transportation company and the city's Traffic Department. The driver refused, fearing potential consequences, including fines and job loss, as the buses are monitored. This was enough to prompt the individuals to shoot him.

The population of Venda Nova, like that of many other neighborhoods, is made up of workers, students, and families who rely on public transportation to get to work, school, or to move around in general. They are affected by these violent acts, which also leave them in a state of indignation. The mood is tense, and there have even been reports of physical aggression between the parties involved.

We cannot close our eyes to the chaos that has been installed. We cannot continue to be exposed to robberies, shots, and deaths, even inside buses. Our patience has reached its limit. We cannot accept children and young people growing up without any sense of fraternity or civility.

It is important that we rethink our relationships, public security, and the creation of a future for our children. One of the murderers is only 14 years old; the other is 19. We cannot allow children and young people to be raised without any sense of fraternity or civility.

During the speech of Dep. Jô Moraes, Mr. Luiz Couto, in accordance with Article 18, Section 2 of the Internal Regulation, left the Presidency, which was then taken over by Mr. Sebastião Bala Rocha.

I would like to thank Dep. Jô Moraes for her speech and express my condolences and solidarity with the family of José Góes dos Santos and all workers in collective transportation in Belo Horizonte.

segments.text:
Apologies to the Brazilian nation for the torture, the disappearance, and the death of so many people. I commend the government for its position. The truth must be revealed, for the truth sets us free. I invite Deputy Fernando Marroni, from the Rio Grande do Sul, PT, to take the floor.

Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Parliamentarians, Brazilians watching on TV, on the last Friday, President Dilma Rousseff and Agriculture Minister Wagner Rossi launched the 2011-2012 Crop Plan. First and foremost, I want to highlight the 107.2 billion reais that will be made available in agricultural credit. That's a record, by the way.

However, in this speech, I want to focus on the Agriculture of Low Carbon (ABC) program. Created in 2010, the new ABC investments, announced by Dilma and Rossi during the Crop Plan launch ceremony, demonstrate that sustainable agriculture has become one of the mainstays of Brazil's agricultural and livestock plan. The ABC program will incorporate all investment programs aimed at efficient, sustainable production. Thus, it will have a budget of 3.15 billion reais in the new Crop Plan. That's 3.15 billion reais, ladies and gentlemen.

From now on, the ABC program will encompass the Commercial Planting and Forest Recovery Program (PROPFLORA) and the Sustainable Agropecuary Production Stimulus Program (PRODUSA). According to Minister Rossi, "the government is taking large steps to make Brazilian agriculture and livestock one of the most innovative in the world." Among the new ABC initiatives are no-till planting, recovery of degraded areas, integrated crop-livestock-forestry, commercial forest planting, and biological nitrogen fixation, and animal waste treatment. And all this, ladies and gentlemen deputies, will be within the reach of the producer, as access to credit will be easier. The ABC program's interest rate is 5.5% per year, the lowest fixed for rural credit for agricultural enterprises. The repayment period can reach 15 years. Producers and cooperatives can contract up to 1 million reais per beneficiary.

The Brazilian government's concern, however, goes beyond Agriculture of Low Carbon. President Dilma announced that she will also increase the crop financing limit, currently set at 650,000 reais, for producers who adopt sustainable practices such as no-till planting, organic agriculture, and those who already have or present a recovery plan for permanent preservation areas (APPs) and legal reserves. This amount can be increased by up to 45%, depending on the techniques used by the producer.

The current electoral model is deeply unjust, as it privileges those with more resources and gives large parties a significant advantage in the distribution of seats. Changes are necessary, but we must be careful not to worsen the current situation.

Let me give you an example. If one party receives 720,000 votes and another 150,000, and ten seats are up for grabs, the party with 720,000 votes will elect nine Deputies, while the party with 150,000 votes will only get one.

This is the distorted way the current legislation calculates representation, which benefits larger parties. This calculation method needs to be changed, regardless of the political system, so that the will of the voters is respected.

Two issues that are not being adequately debated in the political reform hearings concern me. The first is the unjust way seats are distributed. The second is the end of the possibility of alliances in proportional representation.

I have conducted a study in all Brazilian states to assess what the composition of the Federal Deputies would be today if there had been no alliances in the 2010 election.

It is a great joy for me to know that, despite the budget cut, President Dilma guaranteed the investment that will transform our "Água para Todos" (Water for All) program into a national initiative, aiming to serve 5 million families by 2014. This will undoubtedly be one of the marks of our President's management. I am also pleased to inform that the municipality of São José do Egito, in Pernambuco's Pajeú region, governed by socialist Evandro Valadares, where I am the majority deputy, will be the first to implement the "Água para Todos" program in all urban and rural residences by the end of this year.

Northeast Brazil is currently living a special moment, visible beyond our country's borders. A publication in The Economist magazine last month highlighted that the region has been growing at 4.2% annually, surpassing the national average of 3.6%. Last year, Pernambuco's economy experienced a "Chinese" growth of 9.3%. The publication also noted that, in addition to the Bolsa Família (Family Allowance) and Crediamigo (a microcredit program), other initiatives have helped lift over 1 million Northeasterners out of poverty.

I would also like to highlight the extraordinary work being done in Pernambuco by Governor Eduardo Campos and mention one of his initiatives: the "Todos por Pernambuco" (All for Pernambuco) project, which focuses on democratic and regionalized management with a results-oriented approach. This involves a series of seminars covering the twelve microregions of the state, aiming to establish a permanent communication channel between government and society, integrating planning, management, and financial execution to ensure the efficiency of public policies and the satisfaction of citizens' aspirations.

At the meeting of the São Francisco Microrregion in Petrolina, with the presence of National Integration Minister Fernando Bezerra Coelho, Governor Eduardo Campos signed four agreements, representing investments of approximately R$160 million in the São Francisco Microrregion. These included R$94.5 million for water and sanitation works in Petrolina, and R$53.3 million for Ouricuri and Araripi, respectively. The governor concluded the first day of the marathon visit by touring the Gercino Coelho State School, which underwent a complete renovation costing R$1.7 million.

He noted that all commitments made at the first seminar in 2007 had been fulfilled.

Many proposals were put forward, with particular emphasis on family farming, cultural centers, the implementation of urgent care posts (UPAs), and road construction. "We had direct contact with the secretary and I concluded that Mr. [Eduardo Campos] chose very well. He is firm and will do a lot," she said.

The Araripe micro-region comprises the municipalities of Ipubi, Bodoco, Exu, Moreilandia, Granito, Ouricuri, Trindade, Santa Filomena, Santa Cruz, and Araripina. All these cities were represented at the seminar.

- Expansion of water supply systems for Pirapama, Mundaú, and Camevô.

- Requalification of the Batalha and Pan-Nordestina highways.
- Installation of the Grande Recife Consortium.

**EMPLOYMENT**

Women understood the creation of the Straw Hat Project, established in 1988, as a unique opportunity. This project aimed to support and assist thousands of workers and farmers in the sugar cane industry who faced unemployment and wage loss during the off-season.

During the period 2007/2010, 61,637 new job opportunities were generated on average annually, compared to only 32,585 in the previous quadrennium.

The attraction of structural enterprises was increased by 76.5%, with private investments 9.96 times greater than those existing up to 2006.

**Implantation of New Businesses**

In 2010, new enterprises were confirmed in Pernambuco: a car manufacturer (R$3 billion) and a steel mill (R$1.5 billion). A total of 1,049 new companies were established in the state during 2007/2009.

By October 2010, the IPA had assisted 73,319 family farmers with technical assistance and rural extension services.

**SECMULHER AND RURAL WOMEN**

The State of Pernambuco has made significant strides in advancing women's rights. Cristina Buarque, the competent head of the Women's Secretariat, has led an excellent effort in this area.

SECMULHER, along with the methodology applied in the Straw Hat Project for Women, has enabled the secretariat to connect with rural women in the state's interior. Since 2009, the General Coordination for Gender Actions - GERAI has been implementing the "Convert Women" project, serving the 17 municipalities with the lowest IDH in the state, as well as women in Arcoverde.

**NETWORK OF PUBLIC POLICY AGENTS FOR RURAL WOMEN**

The historical urban-rural and male-female hierarchies bring disadvantages to rural populations, particularly in the state's interior. The field and its inhabitants are, in a sense, invisible to public policies.

The network of public policy agents for rural women is based on the demands of women from rural social movements, in their various manifestations and organizations, with the aim of rectifying the historical disadvantages of this segment of the population and facilitating their access to public policies and employment and income opportunities.

The network was initiated in 2007, within the framework of the Straw Hat Project, when SECMULHER conducted the first public policy course involving women from 36 municipalities in the sugar cane region, laying the groundwork for future actions.

Now, dear colleagues, the report referred to grapes as the second most contaminated product with agrochemicals in Brazil.

As a representative from a region where I have lived for almost 40 years, Petrolina and the São Francisco Valley, I would like to speak about the significant contamination of our agricultural products. This news, based on studies conducted by ANVISA, fell into the disastrous and irresponsible error of not disclosing the origin of the products being analyzed. The fact is, without knowing the source of the problem, it is practically impossible to find a solution.

The cultivation of wine grapes, on just 12,000 hectares, generates 72,000 direct jobs in agriculture at the peak of the harvest. This is not just a simple number; it's a reality that cannot be ignored. While soy occupies over 23.6 million hectares nationwide to employ half of these people, 48 million hectares of soy would be needed to employ the same number of people working in the São Francisco Valley's agricultural areas.

To put it into perspective, the total area harvested in the 2010 Brazilian agricultural season was 48.1 million hectares. The annual revenue generated by the São Francisco Valley approaches 2 billion reais. The resources entering the country from the export of mangoes and grapes amount to approximately 500 million reais annually.

The ripple effects of these resources in other economic sectors and their consequent social impacts are extremely relevant for the region. I would like to highlight viticulture, as only in its 12,000 hectares are more than 72,000 direct jobs in agriculture created during the peak of the harvest.

Grapes produced in the São Francisco Valley meet the highest quality standards to meet the most demanding markets worldwide, thanks to efficient production control systems monitored and certified by various quality protocols, such as Tesco, Global GAP, PIF Brazil, among others.

In today's globalized world, news travels rapidly, producing almost instantaneous results worldwide. When the news is negative, originating from disastrous and irresponsible research conducted by a government agency, the consequences can be severe. This was the case with the report broadcast on Globo Repórter by Rede Globo on March 25, 2011.

The program's main focus was the promotion of organic products. Without delving into the discussion about the presentation on this production system, as we believe the report was manipulated and biased (since organic products can be free of chemical contamination but may have biological contamination, especially with fecal matter, a fact not disclosed), the matter presented by this important television program is detrimental to the nation, as it does not specify the material analyzed. General information like this causes doubt and brings harm to the economy of the São Francisco Valley, in the Sertão region of Pernambuco.

Someone must be held responsible for this information.

What is our project?

'The ACS case' is a convergence of strategic interests between two countries. As everyone knows, we not only have, but throughout all of Northern and Northeastern Brazil, the best area on the planet for rocket launches. For two very simple reasons:

(I) In the Alcântara (Maranhão) region, for example, we are at 2.2 degrees south and on the Ceará coast, 3.8 degrees south of the equator (Kourou, in French Guiana, where the European launch center is located, is at 5 degrees north). This significantly increases the tangential velocity of any object on the surface, or in other words, an initial impulse very favorable for equatorial launches, as is the case with communication satellites. This translates into an increase in the carrying capacity of launch vehicles, making them more competitive compared to launches at higher latitudes.

(II) Along our coastline, we have a vast and diverse maritime area, essential for security purposes. Thus, launches can follow simpler, 'flat' trajectories and directly place satellites into orbit, without the need for complex maneuvers, unlike other launch centers. Due to this, some visionary thinkers believed, and still believe, that we have all the conditions to set up a large space-scientific complex. The initial idea was to have, alongside the current Alcântara Launch Center (CLA), operated by the Air Force and dedicated to the VLS, three additional space launch sites capable of operating with other vehicles, in addition to those already under development by an independent program. One of them would be the Cyclone-4, from ACS. We would have as guardians of these sites, and as a result of them, a park of companies supporting space activities, as well as institutions for teaching and research in pure and cutting-edge technology.

As a result of this technical revolution in the region, industrial and service activities would substantially favor the development of the tourist potential of the Maranhão and Louisiana regions.

Let's remember that in 1980, the conception of the CLA provided for the implementation in a vast area of 62,000 hectares, of which only 20,000 would be used for operational purposes (the rest would be for relocation of people, natural reserves, and for the establishment of an industrial support park).
