The land extensions are a security imperative, and as it often happens in the main launch centers worldwide, locations were mobilized to prevent the initial field studies (I refer to the blockade of February 2008). And as if that weren't enough, we were not allowed to remain in the area previously ceded by the Brazilian state.

From here on, reality begins to drift away. A state entity in Brazil, the INCRA, decided that in the Municipality of Alcântara, there was a gigantic quilombola territory, covering approximately 90% of the current municipality's area, excluding the small head with its colonial architecture threatened by neglect.

Two consequences arise from this: first, the ACS was deprived of its area; second, the CLA, whose original conception foreseen dozens of thousands of hectares, was reduced to less than a dozen thousand and lost any chance of expansion.

Access conditions set an exemplary case. The CLA area (where the ACS is installed on leased land to the Aeronautics) is embedded in what is known as the quilombola territory, which results in access to operational areas being conditioned by transit through this territory, of people, equipment, and materials, some carrying hazardous substances (such as propellant components, hydrazine, and tetroxide) circulating through populated areas.

Additionally, the Ministry of Transportation, which oversaw the construction of the port, forgot to allocate the respective funds. For this and incredible reason, we will be forced, to ensure the arrival and disembarkation of materials and equipment, to use a rudimentary pier located more than 50 kilometers from the ACS site. To do so, we have had to improve this entire route. We are reconstructing, with resources from the AEB, the road that connects Cujupe to Alcântara.

And the rocket (ranging from 24.5 to 35 tons when not carrying cargo), coming from Dnepropetrouvsk (Ukraine) to Alcântara by air, is estimated to cost around 1,700 thousand dollars today.

Previously, our main competitor, alongside some foreign NGOs, was an entity called the Palmares Foundation (Ministry of Culture). Armed with arguments that, in principle, aimed to defend the remaining quilombo populations and preserve cultural values, many obstacles were presented to the implementation of the ACS.

Only a few hundred families would be directly affected by the ACS site implementation, but they saw this as an opportunity for improvement.

However, other space programs also deserve attention. China, for example, began in 1956 and sent a man into space in 2003. India has already launched satellites and sondas, the same happening with Israel. South Korea, after the failure of its first launch in 2010, is on the verge of becoming the most recent country to enter the 'launchers club'.

North Korea and Iran are ahead of us. Our first activity as rocket launchers dates back to 1965. We've advanced with a family of suborbital probe vehicles. We've produced and operated small and medium-sized satellites. However, our satellite launcher has not taken off after less than 30 years of efforts. Why not? Are we incompetent, or does God not like Brazilians? The answer is simple: we are the 23rd largest investor in space programs when considering each country's GDP. The resources allocated for investment in the Brazilian space program do not exceed 0.010% of our GDP, that is, about ten times less than France, Russia, and China.

Let's look at our situation compared to the BRICs. Russia invested two billion four hundred million U.S. dollars in its space program in 2009, while we have only 164 million. That's still very little, but we have to acknowledge: investments, which had been declining, were resumed at the beginning of this decade, a reversal led by President Lula's government. When the VLS accident occurred, I gave an interview as Minister of Science and Technology, stating that the VLS project had been fatally hit by a lack of resources. I was criticized by everyone, including government colleagues. In this text, I repeat that assertion, now backed by irrefutable data: the distribution of resources from 1980 to 2009 (the accident, as we know, occurred in 2003) and the conclusions reached by the Parliamentary Inquiry Commission of the Chamber of Deputies, convened to investigate the causes of the accident.

Only in the period from 1985 to 1989 did investments concentrate on the three activity segments - satellites, vehicles, and launch sites - with an average annual investment of 100 million dollars. From 1990 onwards, investments plummeted to 57 million in 1990 and just 9.9 million in 1999. In total, the country spent only US$530.2 million from 1980 to 2002 (the eve of the VLS launch) on space programs. How can we seriously consider launching our VLS if, year after year, the government reduces investments? From US$27.5 million in 1995, we fell to 11.271 million in 1997, 10.408 million in 1998, and finally to US$3.7 million in 2002. In 1999, the government had the audacity to only allocate US$1.6 million!

This is the summary of the attention we are giving to strategic projects. In 26 years of VLS development, our first satellite vehicle, we've made three attempts, three failures. Has the effort been in vain? Of course not, because a lot has been learned and progress has been made. But the accident compromised the pace.

As for the Ukraine, it has one of the world's best rockets, but due to geographical constraints, it lacks a launch site and cannot launch its rockets without flying over other countries, discarding its lower stages. Currently, Ukraine is forced to launch its rockets from Russian and Kazakhstani sites, Plesetsk and Baikonur. On our side, we have excellent areas for launch sites, but we lack a rocket. This is what is called an intersection of interests. The ACS is a space transport company that, in addition to meeting the interests of both countries, can compete, with advantages, in the global market for satellite transport. It is obvious the importance of satellites, but a satellite is not neutral; it is not only for civil use, not only for meteorological purposes, but for almost everything, including intelligence gathering, monitoring borders, monitoring our oil platforms, guiding police and military movements, and remotely controlled weapons. To ensure the functioning of the new air traffic control system, CNS/ATM, requires satellites.

The DNOCS (National Department of Water and Climate) has always managed water resources efficiently and competently, despite limited financial resources, in the specific case of the State of Ceará in northeastern Brazil. This department, established in 1909, has a mature and unquestionable water infrastructure, monitoring 85% of the public and private dams in the state, while COGERH (Ceará State Water Management Company) monitors only 15%.

Out of 130 dams in Ceará, the DNOCS monitors 60, while COGERH monitors 70. For this purpose, with its administrative and human resources, the DNOCS employs only five people, including two engineers. In contrast, COGERH has approximately 500 employees and is announcing a public contest to hire an additional 65 staff. This fact is important to note, demonstrating the responsibility of those in charge for the social and economic success of this undertaking.

The demand for water usage fees and the establishment of an entity to manage this significant project are matters that require careful analysis and deep reflection. Moreover, in a year with good winter rains, the project will undoubtedly not be fully utilized. Similarly, if we experience several years of above-average rainfall, it will remain partially or entirely idle, and there will be no water usage fees. In reality, the São Francisco Project will only operate during critical periods, every two, three, five, or even six years, as has already occurred in our region.

The primary function of this project is to foster synergy in the use of dams in the region, potentially increasing water utilization by approximately 30% of their current capacities. Currently, water reservoirs in northeastern Brazil are operated in a way that does not maximize their potential.

Along the rivers, it expanded slowly; as the main factors of production, land, and capital concentrated, small settlements began to develop. The interior lands of Bahia were granted through land grants to two families—the Garcia d'Ávila and the Guedes de Brito, which marked the origin of land concentration in the region. The 18th century (the cycle of gold) was characterized by the deceleration of the occupation of Western Bahia. In 1701, through a Royal Charter, the government prohibited any connection between the states of Bahia and Minas Gerais through the São Francisco River.

In the 19th century, rivers once again became important links between the sertão (backlands) and the cerrado (savanna) with other regions. Major rivers in the Western region, such as Corrente, Grande, and Preto, grew in importance. In this context, it's worth highlighting the dominant land structure in the region: on one side, large landowners who own extensive latifundia and raise cattle; on the other, small landowners engaged in subsistence agriculture and incipient cattle raising. Colonialism dominated regional politics.

Barra, located in the current Mesorregião do Vale do São Francisco, was the main city in the region. The economic landscape in Western Bahia changed significantly in the second half of the 20th century due to exogenous territorial integration policies by the federal government in the 1960s. Public investments in infrastructure, coupled with tax incentives and low land prices, attracted attention to the region from other areas of the state and, particularly, from other states in the country, notably the Southern Region, where farmers suffered from depleted soils due to predatory agricultural practices and high land prices.

Another decisive factor for intensifying land use is the significant water availability in the Western region. Thus, cattle raising suffered a relative decline, and the region began to be dynamized by grain cultivation, primarily soybeans, accompanied by a diversity of crops such as corn, cotton, rice, among others. Industry is slowly emerging, mainly as a support to primary production, forming small agro-industrial complexes and producing food items.

The Mesorregião do Oeste Baiano benefited from the expansion of the national road network, which facilitated the export of goods produced in the region. Even though this technical network is still incipient for the current growth of the region, it has played a crucial role in its economic development.

Starting in the 1970s, Western Bahia experienced accelerated economic growth, primarily in the primary sector. Notable productions include irrigated coffee, rice, fruit cultivation (using advanced techniques), and cotton, which is one of the largest cotton-producing regions in Latin America. Corn production accounts for 50% of the state's production, with an 80.6% increase in productivity between the 2005/06 and 2006/07 crops (AIBA, 2007).

In the primary sector, irrigated coffee and fruit cultivation stand out, along with rice production.

3 – Historical Formation


In 1840, the area now known as Petrolina was called "Passagem de Juazeiro," a non-inhabited point of convergence for travelers from Ceará, Piauí, and Pernambuco en route to Bahia and the southern regions of the country. This passage served as a meeting point for various regional routes, and by this time, some settlements had begun to emerge to support these travelers.

As a result of this, a small community began to form. In 1862, it was established as a parish and elevated to the status of a village by Law No. 530 of June 7, 1862, named Petrolina in honor of Emperor Dom Pedro II.

Petrolina was later suppressed by provincial law but later restored by Law No. 921 of May 18, 1870. Its reinstatement occurred on May 24 of the same year. It achieved autonomous municipality status on April 25, 1893. By Law No. 130 of July 3, 1895, Petrolina was elevated to the category of city and officially installed on September 25, 1895.

4 – Infrastructure

Petrolina stands out from the 1980s as the beginning of more pronounced development. During this decade, the primary and secondary sectors were intensively dynamized through the implementation of major irrigation projects by the Company for the Development of the São Francisco Valley (CODEVASF) and the establishment of agroindustries.

The municipality of Petrolina boasts a robust infrastructure, with indicators surpassing those of many other Brazilian municipalities.

The city's sanitation system, however, only reaches approximately 60% of the population. There are still several areas without proper sanitation, including all districts and neighborhoods in the municipality's interior, as well as specific neighborhoods like Jardim Imperial, Portal da Cidade, Alto do Cocar, Vale do Grande Rio, Pedra Linda, Henrique Leite, Fernado Idalino, Vila Marcela, Vila Carolina (IPSEP I), Dom Avelar, Santa Luzia, and various other subdivisions.

**Petrolina's Irrigation and Urban Development**

Areas known as "sequeiro," typical of the Northeastern semi-arid region, contrast with irrigated lands resulting from public and private investments in irrigation technology, initiated in the late 1960s with the Bebedouro Project as a pilot. This was followed by the Senator Nilo Coelho Project, the extension of km 25, now Maria Teresa, and the South and North Pontal Projects, simultaneously with private investments. The municipality currently has approximately 60,000 hectares (54% public and 46% private) of irrigated land.

The region primarily produces mango (9,800 hectares), grape (8,800 hectares), sugarcane (10,500 hectares), tomato (1,500 hectares), and, to a lesser extent, banana (4,864 hectares), acerola (5,500 hectares), asparagus (700 hectares), and others like pine, coconut, passion fruit, guava, etc.

Irrigation has had a socio-economic impact by promoting changes in the existing technical base. The "sequeiro" area, inserted into the socio-economic context of the Northeastern semi-arid region, faces challenges related to the sustainability of economic activities. One of the main problems for human survival is water supply in terms of quality, quantity, distribution, and temporal availability—a constant or reliable supply.

Economic and social activities based on water resources from watering holes have shown that this is not a permanent solution. During longer dry periods, emergency measures are always required. Extensive livestock farming requires an area that does not align with the current land use situation. Technology needs to be incorporated into this process to adapt to the new spatial reality.

In the social sphere, the presence of public services, higher family income, and smaller geographical area distinguish the urban zone of Petrolina, with two naturally distinct areas: the center and the neighborhoods. Considering population indicators, infrastructure, public services, income level, economic activity intensity, and geographical extent, the area of the neighborhoods meets the greatest basic needs.

Subregionalization indicates, through the same indicators, that the North Zone is the most deprived, followed by the West. People so destitute that they did not even register for well-known social programs like Bolsa Família. Far less do they have access to essential services like water, electricity, education, health, and housing.

The 2010 Census by IBGE showed that in the North and Northeast, 16 million Brazilians live below the poverty line, meaning a per capita income of R$70 per month. This led Brazil to launch, starting today, its largest integrated plan to combat extreme poverty in its history.

At a ceremony held at the Planalto Palace, President Dilma Rousseff launched the "Brazil Without Poverty" plan, which coordinates efforts by the Federal Government, States, and Municipalities to improve the lives of 16 million Brazilians.

Led by the Ministry of Social Development and Hunger Combat, the plan deepens and expands the successful social policies adopted by Brazil in recent years, when 28 million people rose out of poverty and 36 million entered the middle class.

Now, the focus is on the 16 million Brazilians whose family income, divided among its members, does not exceed R$70 per person per month. Of this total, 59% live in the Northeast, 21% in the South and Southeast, and 20% in the North and Central-West. And 40% are under 14 years old.

In addition to its humanitarian aspect, the plan aims to be a powerful lever for Brazil's development. After all, the process of social advancement over the last 8 years has been decisive in reducing inequalities, expanding the internal market, strengthening the economy, and accelerating the country's growth. With the "Brazil Without Poverty" plan, the government takes on the challenge of ending poverty and thus takes a new and decisive step to expand these achievements for all Brazilians.

The state reaching where poverty is located: In recent years, the Brazilian government has drawn closer to the poorest than ever before. Thus, 28 million Brazilians have risen out of absolute poverty and 36 million have entered the middle class.

Even with this effort, 16 million people still remain in extreme poverty. Among other reasons, because there is a poverty so poor that it is difficult to reach through state action. It is as if it were hidden in remote corners.

Public programs like Bolsa Família, Rural Previdence, Brazil Alfabetizado, Family Health, Brazil Smiles, More Education, and the Baby Care Network, among others, will be expanded and improved throughout the country, as well as actions to increase access for the poorest to public goods, including water, electricity, and housing.

To achieve these goals, the plan is creating the most comprehensive Poverty Map of Brazil. And it is also drawing up an Opportunity Map to identify the most appropriate and efficient means to improve the lives of these people.

**TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE**

The poorest farmers will receive continued and individualized assistance from teams of professionals hired primarily in their local regions by the Federal Government. Each group of 1,000 families will be assisted by one senior technician and ten mid-level technicians. A partnership with universities and EMBRAPA will introduce appropriate technologies to each family, increasing their production.

**PROMOTION AND SEEDS**

Brazil Without Poverty will support extremely poor families in food production and the commercialization of their production. Each family will receive a grant of R$2,400, paid in semi-annual installments over two years, to purchase inputs and equipment. By 2014, 250,000 families will have been assisted. The plan includes other complex actions in addition to the promotion, such as the provision of EMBRAPA seeds and appropriate technologies for each region.

**WATER FOR ALL**

The goal here is to provide 750,000 families with construction of cisterns and simplified collection systems. Additionally, thousands of families will be benefited by water systems designed for production.

**PROGRAM TO ACQUIRE FOOD (PAA)**

PAA is one of the most effective programs in expanding the market for small farmers. Attracting them, the Federal Government purchases their production to donate to charitable institutions or for the formation of reserves. With Brazil Without Poverty, PAA will be significantly expanded. Currently, it assists 66,000 families, and by 2014, it is expected to reach 250,000 families.

**RESULT OF THE PROGRAM**

Aiming for the productive inclusion of the poorest population, Brazil Without Poverty will, among other actions, promote the articulation of various governmental programs. The goal is to create new opportunities for 2 million people.

For 30 years, since I arrived in the state of Pará, I have been a proponent of agrarian reform in the Amazon. Family farming development in the Amazon will only be possible if settlements are made along rivers or highways.

The state of Pará currently has over 5,000 kilometers of federal highways, many already paved, with others in the process of being paved, such as the Cuiabá-Santarém and Transamazônica highways. By the end of 2014, these two highways, covering 2,000 kilometers, will likely be fully paved.

The government could purchase lands along these highways and allocate them for family settlement. This way, energy, healthcare, education, and transportation would be more accessible, and the cost of goods would be lower.

Currently, the opposite is happening: what is produced is sold at a lower price, and what families need to buy costs more. This exchange leads to impoverishment, de-capitalization, and the failure of many families settled by the INCRA.

Another critical issue is infrastructure. Merely implementing the "Light for All" program, a commendable initiative, is not enough. We need to advance in providing electricity to all communities. **BILL NO. 1.655, 2011**

(From Mrs. Professor Dorinha Seabra Rezende)

Amending § 1 of Article 15 of Law No. 9.424, of December 24, 1996, regarding the national distribution of salary-education resources.

The National Congress decrees:

**ARTICLE 1**

§ 1 of Article 15 of Law No. 9.424, of December 24, 1996, is amended as follows:

"§ 1. The amount collected from the salary-education tax, after deducting 1% for the Federal Revenue Secretariat, calculated based on the amount collected by it, shall be distributed by the National Education Development Fund (FNDE) among the states and the Federal District in the following proportions:

I. A quota for the Union, corresponding to one-third of the total amount of resources, to be allocated to the FNDE for financing projects and actions aimed at universalizing basic education;

II. A quota for the states, the Federal District, and municipalities, corresponding to two-thirds of the total amount, distributed proportionately based on the number of students enrolled in their respective basic education networks, as per the census data from the Ministry of Education."

**JUSTIFICATION**

The purpose of this bill is to transform the federal salary-education revenue, currently distributed in a way that benefits wealthier states and municipalities, into an effective tool for resource redistribution. Currently, two-thirds of the state quota is returned to the state where the revenue was collected. The richer regions receive more resources, while the poorer ones essentially share the misery. This does not contribute to the eradication of existing inequalities in the country.

The proposed bill ensures a national average per student for salary-education resources, promoting a more equitable distribution among the federative entities.

I am convinced that the importance of this matter will be recognized by the esteemed colleagues, who will provide the necessary support for its approval.

**Legislative Act**

**Article 1:** People affected by neuromuscular diseases with motor paralysis shall receive priority access to the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS) for essential medications and equipment aimed at their survival, including those necessary for comorbidities. This law prioritizes the treatment of individuals with neuromuscular diseases, particularly those with motor paralysis. Numerous conditions fall under this category, and the established priority ensures access only for those whose health condition poses a risk to their survival. The primary focus of this legislation is the protection of life through the prioritized distribution of medications and equipment.

**§1:** The list of neuromuscular diseases with motor paralysis to be covered by this law shall be defined by the executive branch through a specific act.

**§2:** The executive branch, through the Ministry of Health, shall select the medications and equipment mentioned in the lead sentence, to guide their acquisition by SUS managers.

**§3:** The selection referred to in §2 shall be reviewed and republished annually or whenever necessary to align with current scientific knowledge and the availability of new medications, technologies, and products in the market.

**Article 2:** Medications and equipment required for patients under this law may be delivered to their respective residences previously registered with competent health authorities, without any cost to the patient.

**Single Paragraph:** A partnership agreement may be established between the competent SUS authority and state or municipal health entities in the District of Federal for the prioritized delivery of medications and equipment to individuals affected by neuromuscular diseases with motor paralysis.

**Article 3:** Non-profit entities that operate in this area and hold social assistance beneficiary certification under existing legislation may enter into a partnership agreement with the competent SUS authority or state or District of Federal entities, or municipal entities conveniated with the SUS, for the delivery of equipment and care to individuals affected by neuromuscular diseases with motor paralysis.

**Article 4:** Individuals affected by neuromuscular diseases with motor paralysis have the right to receive, in writing, within 48 hours of their request, information regarding the unavailability of medications and equipment from the same health authority.

**Article 5:** The Union shall promote scientific research, including gene therapy, aimed at preventing, treating, and curing neuromuscular diseases with motor paralysis.

**Article 6:** This law shall enter into force on the first day of the next fiscal year following its publication.

NEURAL INJURIES OF THE BRACHIAL PLEXUS

The distinction is important, as most lesions with unfavorable progression occur in complete lesions that persist for 2 to 3 months or more.

Since the upper end receives its motor and sensory nerves entirely from the brachial plexus, injuries to the brachial plexus can present with a wide variety of clinical manifestations, depending on the portion affected.

Supraclavicular injuries to the brachial plexus are usually subdivided into preganglionic (supraganglionic, intradural) and postganglionic (infraganglionic, extradural, extraforaminal) types.

Lesions above the clavicle are further subdivided into "upper plexus" (involving the ventral branches of C5 and C6) and "lower plexus" (involving the ventral branches of C8 and T1). C7 represents the "water divider" between the two types of paralysis and is typically unaffected in either.

Lesions can be partial (incomplete) or complete.

**NEUROPATIES**

Neuropathies can be classified based on axonal or demyelinating involvement, as well as the clinical presentation, which can be acute, subacute, or chronic. When a single nerve is affected, it's considered a mononeuropathy. Involvement of multiple nerves in a symmetric and simultaneous manner is termed polyneuropathy.

Clinical manifestations may be motor, sensory, or autonomic, with distal symptomatology predominant.

**Abnormalities in Sensitivity**

These can present as paresthesia (alteration in sensation), hyperesthesia (increased sensitivity to stimuli, often unpleasant), hypoesthesia (reduced sensitivity to touch or painful stimuli), or dysesthesias (altered perception of stimuli).

**Mononeuropathy Multiplex and Polyneuropathy**

These conditions can clinically manifest with physical weakness.

**MONONEUROPATHY MÚLTIPLA**

Primary causes include leprosy, vasculitis, diabetes, and sarcoidosis.

**POLINEUROPATIA PERIFÉRICA - AXONAL AGUDA**

Acute axonal neuropathy is characterized by physical weakness.

**Notable Example:** Acute intermittent porphyria, an autosomal dominant disorder caused by impaired heme synthesis.

**POLINEUROPATIA PERIFÉRICA - AXONAL SUBACUTA**

Notable causes include toxic and drug-induced agents, malnutrition, uremia, diabetes, rheumatic diseases (Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, Rheumatoid Arthritis), hypothyroidism, AIDS, sarcoidosis, and paraneoplastic syndromes.

**HEREDITARY SENORY MOTOR NEUROPATHIES**

Type I (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease) and Type III (Dejerine-Sottas disease) are primary representatives. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is the most common hereditary neuropathy in adults, characterized by typical lower limb atrophy.

**DIAGNOSTIC SCHEME FOR DIFFERENT FORMS OF NEUROPATHIES**

The diagnostic approach considers clinical manifestations, laboratory tests, and nerve conduction studies.

**GENETIC NEUROPATHIES**

**PORPHYRIC NEUROPATHY:**  In most cases, it is an acute peripheral neuropathy of predominantly motor origin, often associated with exacerbation of porphyrin symptoms, including abdominal pain, vomiting, tachycardia, and also confusional state and seizures. The acute onset is usually precipitated by drugs, particularly barbiturates, oral contraceptives, and alcohol.  Neuropathy first affects the upper extremities, with the lower extremities less involved. There is a long list of triggers, including alcohol, sulfa, and phenitoin.

**FAMILIAL AMYLOIDOSIS (Corino de Andrade disease):** The most important familial amyloidosis is of the Portuguese or Corino de Andrade type, which has an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. The disease begins insidiously between 25 and 35 years of age, with sensory and dysesthetic symptoms in the lower extremities.  Later, plantar fascinating pain develops and walking becomes difficult. The autonomic nervous system is severely affected. This is one of the characteristic features of the disease, leading to sexual impotence, postural hypotension, and diarrhea.  Superficial sensitivity is significantly impaired compared to deep sensitivity, which remains relatively normal. The progression is progressive and fatal after 10 to 20 years from onset. There is no proven specific treatment.

**AUTONOMIC NEUROPATHIES - SENSITIVELY TYPE:**  Rare and predominantly manifest as painless plantar malformations. As the condition is initially only sensory, with no trophic changes, it can be difficult to characterize the organicity of the manifestations.

**AUTONOMIC NEUROPATHIES - MOTOR TYPE (Charcot-Marie-Tooth):**  Atrophy of peroneal muscles and variants (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease - CMT) is a heterogeneous group of hereditary peripheral neuropathies, usually with autosomal dominant inheritance, characterized by slowly progressive impairment. Symptoms begin in childhood or adolescence. The intrinsic muscles of the feet and peroneal muscles are the first to weaken, leading to legs appearing like champagne bottles inverted. As the disease progresses, atrophy of hand intrinsic muscles and muscles below the knees almost disappear.  Tendinous reflexes are diminished or absent, particularly in the lower extremities. Muscle strength and trophism decrease, eventually leading to irreversible destruction of affected axons. Early diagnosis in mononeuropathy or multiple mononeuropathy is essential to preserve nerve integrity, even if there is no skin lesion indicating porphyrin disease.

**HANSEATIS:** The neurological picture of leprosy varies according to its polarity. Tubercular leprosy presents as mononeuropathy or multiple mononeuropathy, with the ulnar, radial, peroneal, median, and posterior tibial nerves most affected. The nerve to palpation is thickened and very painful. The disease begins with pain, numbness, and paresthesias in the affected nerve distribution, leading to muscle weakness, atrophy, and finally, irreversible destruction of the affected axons.
June 2011                      JOURNAL OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES                        Thursday 23   32367

**VIRCHOWIAN FORM: **The involvement of nerves presents as symmetric distal polyneuropathy and is not paraneoplastic. The most affected regions are the colder parts of the body (ears, dorsal surfaces of hands and feet, anterodorsal surface of forearms, and anterolateral surface of legs), with sensory distal polyneuropathy and symmetric distal sensory-motor polyneuropathy being the two main types.

**DIMORPHIC AND INDETERMINATE FORMS:** The clinical picture can vary widely, from the tuberculoid pole to the virchovian pole.

**DIABETES MELLITUS:** Diabetic neuropathy affects approximately 50% of patients with diabetes, especially those with a long history of poorly controlled glycemia (above 180 mg/dL). It's important to note that neuropathy can also occur in individuals with glucose intolerance.

**TYPES OF DIABETIC NEUROPATHY:**

* **Sensory:**  Affects the ability to feel touch, temperature, and pain.

* **Motor:**  Impairs muscle strength and movement.

* **Autonomic:**  Affects involuntary functions like heart rate, blood pressure, and digestion.

* **Mononeuropathy:**  Affects a single nerve (often cranial nerves)

* **Multineuropathy:** Affects multiple nerves simultaneously.

The most common type is distal symmetric sensory-motor polyneuropathy, usually associated with diabetes. However, it can be the *initial* sign of the disease.  Muscle weakness is not common.

**ASSOCIATED WITH COLAGEN DISEASES AND VASCULITIS:**

Collagen diseases like periarterite nodosa (PAN) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) frequently cause peripheral neuropathies.  Other collagen diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma, giant cell arteritis, and Wegener's granulomatosis, can also produce them.

**ALCOHOLISM:**  Causes insidious onset of symmetric distal sensory-motor polyneuropathy, affecting lower extremities more than upper.

**PARANEOPLASMIC:** Various types of malignancies can cause peripheral neuropathies by distant effects. Lung, breast, ovarian, myeloma, lymphoma, and lymphosarcoma are the most common types to produce peripheral neuropathies.

**DRUG-INDUCED NEUROPATHY:** Numerous medications can cause peripheral neuropathies of various types. Some examples include:

* Chemotherapeutic agents
* Anticonvulsants
* Antibiotics
* Immunosuppressants

In the State of Rio de Janeiro, Judge Roberto Câmara Lacé Brandão cited in his decision the argument of the Public Ministry that "the situation initially presented as a peaceful political manifestation, in truth, masks an orchestrated action through the diffusion of drug consumption," which "would constitute the crime of advocating drug trafficking."

Freedom cannot be confused with liberty, advocacy of a criminal act, and preaching freedom of expression without respecting the legal order. Freedom of expression, therefore, has legal and moral limits.

**Rationale for the Legislative Decree**

On June 15, 2011, the Supreme Federal Court (STF) accepted, in a decision on Argument of Fundamental Precept Non-Compliance (ADPF) 187, which recognizes the constitutionality of the so-called "Marcha da Maconha" (Cannabis March), that the article 287 of the Brazilian Penal Code, which criminalizes public advocacy of criminal acts, does not apply to peaceful protests for cannabis legalization. Following the vote of the rapporteur, Minister Celso de Mello, the Court gave a constitutional interpretation to the Penal Code provision to distance any understanding that such marches constitute advocacy of a crime.

For the justices present at the session, in these cases, freedom of expression and assembly prevails.

The aforementioned decision, due to its legal nature, has binding effect and reaches the entire society. In less technical terms, it means that, from the date of this decision, groups advocating for cannabis and other psychoactive substances' legalization can hold rallies without being characterized as advocating a crime.

The highest organ of the Judiciary considered that article 287 of the Brazilian Penal Code does not apply in the case of cannabis legalization protests:

"Article 287: Publicly praising a criminal fact or its author.

Penalty: 3 to 6 months' imprisonment or a fine."

This Legislative Decree Project aims to suspend, based on the competence of the National Congress, as established in articles 49, paragraphs V and XI of the Federal Constitution, the effects of the Supreme Federal Court's decision in Argument of Fundamental Precept Non-Compliance (ADPF) No. 187, which recognized the constitutionality of the so-called "Marcha da Maconha."

Without delving into the merits of the issue, it is observed that the Supreme Federal Court exceeded its power to interpret a constitutional norm, as established in article 102, paragraph I, letter a), of the Federal Constitution.

## Subject: OVNIs and/or Underwater Non-Identified Objects (UNOIs) in Varginha

**3. Declassified Material:**

Although the convoy of military trucks generated by the Navy appears to have gone to Varginha for mechanical services days before the same events were to be conducted at the Automaco concessionaire in Três Corações/MG, what is not detailed in the investigation reports from the Civil House of the Brazilian Presidency (2008) regarding the existence of UFO-related documents within the three armed forces, as requested by this Chamber of Deputies in 2010.

**3.1 Testimonies:**

The statements from witnesses identified as "1st Military," "2nd Military," and "3rd Military," recorded and in possession of various UFO researchers who investigated the Varginha case, raise questions regarding the Ministry of Defense's knowledge of these testimonies.

**3.2  Inconsistencies:**

Why wasn't the military personnel directly involved in the Varginha UFO sightings and captures, including students Kátia Andrade Xavier, Fátima da Silva, and Valquíria Aparecida da Silva, as well as lower-ranking military members from the Fire Department Military Corps (CBM) and Military Police (PM) of Minas Gerais, heard during the internal investigation (IPM) No. 18/97 opened at the Army Sergeant School (EsSA)?

**3.3  Confusion and Misinformation:**

The Army's official version regarding the witness "1st Military," particularly regarding the timing and morphological descriptions of the observed creatures, raises questions. According to the documents from IPM (pages 219, 220, 261, 322, 323, 324, 325, 326, 327, and 328), taken during the investigation for conclusions, the creature observed in the afternoon of January 20, 1996, by the students might have been a confusion with "Sr. Mudinho" rather than an extraterrestrial being.

**3.4  The First Encounter:**

If the Army indeed received the first UFO-related creature (CBM) in the morning of January 20, 1996, as claimed by "1st Military," what happened to it afterward? Where are the documents or any other formats of data regarding these information, and what is the current classification of their secrecy?

**3.5  The Investigation:**

The investigation opened by General Sérgio Pedro Coelho Lima, Commander of EsSA, just six days after a press conference held at the lawyer Ubirajara Franco Rodrigues' home, with the stated purpose of "investigating facts regarding news published in the press about the involvement of military personnel from that school in the capture of the 'Varginha ET'," raises questions.

**3.6  Pressure and Retaliation:**

Why did the Commander initiate a second investigation (IPM), eight months later, after the first one concluded without any military personnel from EsSA being punished for any illicit actions? Was it to determine if the authors of the book "Incidente em Varginha – Criaturas do Espaço no Sul de Minas" (Varginha Incident - Space Creatures in Southern Minas), Vitório Pacaccini and Maxs Portes, had committed new illicit actions, repeating what had already been said in the press, by ufologists, and investigated by the first internal investigation?

**3.7  Military Operations:**

Besides the internal investigations and the IPM, did the Brazilian Army conduct any other internal procedures or in collaboration with other government institutions, such as the Fire Department or the Military Police of Minas Gerais, using their logistical capabilities in those initial months of 1996 in Varginha and its surroundings? If so, what were the results?

On April 20, 2010, this parliamentarian received the transfer of responses from Minister of Defense Dr. Nelson Jobim to Information Request No. 4470 of 2009 (RIC 4470/2009) from the First Secretariat. The request, submitted by petitioners, sought public information regarding UFO (unidentified flying object) inquiries from various ministries, including the Ministry of Defense, based on studies by UFO phenomenon researchers.

The petitioners invoked Law No. 111/2005 of 2007 to demand the complete fulfillment of their request, but two years later, the demand was not fully met. Given the delay by the Ministry in applying legal directives, the commission formed by UFO phenomenon researchers, recognized even by the Brazilian Air Force, requested legislative intervention to expedite and fully address their request.

The response from the Minister included affirmations that all documents related to the UFO subject, which had some level of secrecy, had been declassified due to the expiration of the legal term. The Central of Documentation and Historical of the Brazilian Air Force (CENDOC), responsible for UFO-related matters within its Ministry, was set to close its archives on August 31, 2010, and transfer its entire collection to the Regional Archive Coordination of the Federal District (COREG).

However, after the specified term, several pending issues remained, and new requests emerged. Moreover, it was discovered that not all information related to Operation Prato, the most famous military investigation into extraterrestrial activity in Brazilian airspace, had been made public. While the Air Force (FAB) had been more open to discussing the release of UFO-related information, there remained uncertainty regarding the extent of its archives and how much it was willing to disclose.

In the 1950s, the widely discussed "Trindade Island Flying Saucer" case (items "e" and "f" of § 14 - UFO Brazil Dossier) was fully exposed by Brazilian and international press for several months in 1958 and even in subsequent years. Regarding this case, it is imperative to state that the National Library of Rio de Janeiro has ample historical-journalistic information, preserved in microfilmed copies of contemporary newspapers, proving the episode and the involvement of the institutions mentioned.

However, the main argument that allows us to affirm, at least, the generation of official documents by the Brazilian Navy regarding the Trindade Island Case contradicts categorically the aforementioned certificate No. 60-3/2010 from the Navy. The case occurred on May 5, 1980, near the city of Parintins/AM, over the Amazon River, as registered by the 4th Naval District and communicated to the 2nd Section of I COMAR, through Report (A-1) No. 005 of January 19, 1981, and is registered in the Intelligence Service of the Brazilian Air Force (FAB).

The smuggling, theft, and robbery of vehicles, which only intensify in two of the most active and threatening segments of Brazil's vast border, have become profitable economic activities for the neighboring countries Bolivia and Paraguay.

Decisions by the governments of these two countries have created mechanisms that enable the legalization of stolen vehicle fleets circulating in their territories, thus incorporating criminal products into tax revenue sources.

Paraguayan law exempts its police from investigating the provenance of vehicles, but allows the former owner to go to the country to prove that the item belonged to them.

The Bolivian law says nothing about investigating provenance. It simply charges a fee to register the vehicle without any reference to the possibility of investigation or recovery.

The two cases reflect unilateral decisions by the neighboring governments, given the knowledge of the illicit activities that flourish in these areas, as well as the alleged difficulties of their surveillance systems.

There have been other incidents. In January 2009, Minister of Mines and Energy Edson Lobão was also defeated by Morales over a new contract for gas imports that would inject billions of dollars into Bolivia's coffers.

Evo Morales might argue that he is not the first. He has the precedent of Paraguay, where a similar measure was adopted in January 2001 based on a law passed five years earlier in 1995. The two initiatives differ in their implementation: one established by a law passed by Congress, the other by a presidential decree. Paraguay's measure conditioned legalization on a subsequent confirmation of a registry made available for the former owner to present evidence that the vehicle was his. Bolivia's aim is merely to raise US$ 200 million through fees charged for granting pardons.

Both initiatives share a common goal: to turn stolen vehicles into a source of revenue and to signal alarmingly that these two countries do not have, nor do they announce, an effective mechanism to combat the schemes and gangs that sustain this type of crime. According to information from Veja magazine of January 17, 2001, since the law took effect in October 2000, 1,500 irregular vehicles have been registered in the program for legalization. Estimates suggest that 60% of the 500,000 vehicles in Paraguay's fleet are stolen from Brazil. Local police estimate that at least 20,000 Brazilian-stolen cars enter the country annually.

Recent reports by Fantástico, TV Globo, exposed the fragility of Brazil's control systems along its extensive border, with testimonies from public agents who work within these systems about their inadequate logistical resources and personnel to confront the organized, audacious, and increasingly daring criminal organizations.

REQUEST No. 2.253, 2011

(From Mr. Paes Landim)

Requests that Bill No. 3,405, 1997, be sent to the Commission on Finance and Taxation, in addition to the commissions mentioned in the initial dispatch.

Honorable President,

Decree No. 6,944, 2009, establishes organizational measures for the enhancement of federal direct public administration, autonomous and foundation, and also provides general norms regarding public contests.

The normative aims to strengthen institutional capacity through the conduct of public contests and the provision of public positions (inciso III of § 2 of Article 1) and clarifies the need for evaluation by the Ministry of Planning, Budget and Management (§ 2 of Article 1) of proposals regarding public contests, including their budgetary-financial impacts in the exercise that comes into effect and in the two subsequent exercises (Article 5).

Due to the need to analyze these impacts, the authority to conduct public contests and decide on the provision of public positions and jobs was delegated to the Minister of State for Planning, Budget and Management (Article 10).

In addition, as established by Article 15 of the aforementioned legal norm, it is the responsibility of the same ministry to determine the value charged for contest registration based on the estimated costs indispensable for its conduct.

Furthermore, as established by Article 18 of the substitute offered by the Commission on Constitution and Justice and of Citizenry, while the participants in the contest are required to possess a valid ID, the law does not specify the type of ID, which can be a driver's license, a passport, or any other official document. This opens the door for potential fraud, as individuals without the required qualifications could use false documents to participate.

By privileging individuals with public notarial delegations, whether through a requirement for contest participation, by forcing the prioritization of matters related to the daily activities of notaries in the tests, or by favoring the filling of vacancies for notaries, the bill inhibits the participation of Brazilians who do not hold such delegations.

**MR. SPEAKER,**

I request, in accordance with Article 114, item XIV, in conjunction with Article 86, paragraph 3, of the Internal Regulation, the creation of a Special Committee to issue a report on the Project of Law No. 1,258, 1995, which establishes criteria for telephone tapping or listening (“bugging”) for criminal investigation or judicial proceedings. The Federal Constitution of 1988 is also addressed in this project.

**ROOM OF COMMITTEE, June 22, 2011** – João Campos, Deputy

**JUSTIFICATION**

The creation of this Special Committee is of fundamental importance, not only for fulfilling our constitutional duties, but also because the subject matter has been extensively debated by the Secret Congress Commission on Illegal Phone Tapping (CPI das Escutas Telefônicas Clandestinas) from 2007 to 2009.

For these reasons, we advocate for the approval of this request.

The 1988 Federal Constitution does not explicitly provide for the explicit protection of physical integrity, but this is addressed through Article 5, Section 2, which states that the rights and guarantees expressed in the Constitution do not exclude others derived from the regime and principles it adopts, or from international treaties in which the Federal Republic of Brazil is a signatory.

International conventions that Brazil is a party to, such as the American Convention on Human Rights (San José Agreement), establish in Article 5 the right to personal integrity, where every individual has the right for their physical, psychological, and moral integrity to be respected.

In summary, Article 5 of the American Convention on Human Rights, complementing the Constitution, ensures through Article 5, Section 2, the unrestricted and effective protection of physical integrity as a fundamental right guaranteed by constitutional legislation.

Also noteworthy is that, under the chairmanship of Honorable Deputy Nelson Pellegrino, in the Committee on Constitution and Justice and Citizenship, the Bill No. 6,113 of 2009, after receiving a report highlighting that the text examined, for not meeting the requirements of legality and good legislative technique, required amendments from the Committee, was not included for merit review by the CCJC due to a directive from the House Director, making it impossible to address the aforementioned issues. The rapporteur then presented a second report without corrections to the Senate-originated Bill of Law.

These arguments demonstrate the Committee's competence to express its view on the merits of the proposal.

Therefore, based on the provisions of subparagraphs "d" and "e" of Article 32, Item IV of the House's Rules, I request the redistribution of Bill No. 6,113 of 2009, which "amends the wording of Article 193 of the Consolidated Laws of Work – CLT, approved by Decree-Law No. 5,452 of May 1st, 1943, regarding the activities or operations considered hazardous," for analysis on the merits in the Committee on Constitution and Justice and Citizenship.

We, for another year, have been working with this House's consultants on a proposal that could be the new regulatory framework for Brazil's mineral sector. I believe this House and the Government cannot further delay the debate on this important topic for current and future generations.

I would like to highlight that this Notebook consolidates studies carried out within the Legislative Consulting Office, as we mentioned, and also the contributions of participants in a seminar held in the TV Câmara auditorium in December of last year, where the topic of mineral activity was discussed.

However, many end up blaming the sector itself, stating it's a "Brazilian deindustrialization," characterized by the technological depletion of productive chains. And that's exactly what we want to contest—contest with the phrase of President Luiz Aubert of ABIMAQ: "Brazil is not competitive." It's not the industry that's not competitive; it becomes non-competitive due to issues linked to Brazil as a whole, such as the overvalued real, high interest rates, inadequate infrastructure that hasn't kept pace with industrial sector development, in short, the infamous "Custo Brasil" (Brazil Cost) and the extremely high tax burden in Brazil. That's what's holding it back; that's the real Brazilian disease, not the disease of the Brazilian industry.

Nevertheless, in recent years, the growth of our exports has resulted in a much narrower technical progress, as in the case of agriculture, livestock, and even more so in mining, than would be possible if exports of Brazilian manufactured goods had grown or maintained their previous participation in our trade balance. This is due to the effects of supply chains and the way technical progress is absorbed in primary sectors. In other words, the gain in productivity is much lower in these sectors.

For instance, what happens in a segment of fine chemicals, the result of technology developed outside the country, such as modern agricultural inputs, more modern fertilizers, efficient seeds, and efficient genetic matrices, is all much more linked to agriculture and livestock than to the industrial economic sector, and highly dependent on international monopolies.

The effects are more contained by sector than the technological advancement when it occurs in the industrial sector that permeates everything, spreading into service sectors, requiring better education of the workforce, better engineering services, more technologically advanced urban equipment, better training and workforce qualification.

However, many end up blaming the sector itself, saying it's a "Brazilian deindustrialization," characterized by the technological depletion of productive chains. And that's exactly what we want to contest.

According to the Brazilian Institute of Economy - IBRE, from the Getúlio Vargas Foundation, in a letter titled "The Brazilian Deindustrialization Debate," many economists frequently point to factors such as the real's appreciation, the global financial crisis, and what they call the "China effect," referring to Asia's country bet on emerging markets and, sometimes, unfair competition from its manufactured goods with our products.

"In the light of international experience, until 2008, the deindustrialization process in Brazil was occurring within the norm," comments the letter. Indeed, the participation of imported manufactured goods has been steadily increasing.

In the Brazilian market, growth is increasing, as stated by entity representative Fernando Úmbria. As an example, export volumes have fallen. Excluding vehicle charges, current export levels are 25% lower than three years ago. Moreover, in the last eight years, retail sales have outpaced industrial growth in every year. The volume of Brazilian exports to the United States, our primary destination for manufactured goods, was 36% lower last year compared to the pre-crisis period.

It's possible that this phenomenon is attributable to the contraction of the US economy. Our exports to Japan and Europe have also not returned to pre-crisis levels.

The reflection of a brutal consumption contraction in the US and a strong expansion here has led our industry and theirs to redirect products to the Brazilian market. Meanwhile, our exports to China—the world's fastest-growing country and our primary importer of raw materials—have increased by 77% since the crisis, not just in quantity but also in price gains.

In recent years, however, the growth in our exports has resulted in a much narrower spread of technical progress, as seen in agriculture, livestock, and especially mining, where the benefits of technological advancements are not reaching the broader workforce.

For instance, in the fine chemicals sector, driven by technology developed outside the country, such as modern agricultural inputs, fertilizers, or more efficient seeds, the links to the industrial sector are weak. This is because these products are highly dependent on international oligopolies.

The effects are more contained at the sector level compared to technological advancements in the industrial sector that permeate everything, spreading to service sectors and requiring better-educated workforces, improved engineering services, and more advanced urban equipment.

Other peculiar aspects of Brazil contribute to the infamous "Custo Brasil" (Brazilian Cost). Electricity tariffs have increased by at least 100% in real terms, above the inflation rate for the period. The Brazilian Cost is further compounded by a range of charges that bear little relation to energy activities.

The Brazilian Association of Energy and Environmental Companies (ABRACE) criticizes this situation, stating, "Most of these charges are not directly related to energy activities."

**Bill No. 1 - 009/1999 (Enio Bacci)** - Authorizes the entry into force of the Brazilian Traffic Code, establishing a device to record data on vehicle movement and activation of commands as mandatory equipment for motor vehicles.

**Bill No. 2 - 121/1999 (Raimundo Gomes de Matos)** - Adds a paragraph to Article 5 of Law No. 7.827, of September 27, 1989, naming the Núbia Brasileiro Women's Hospital in Fortaleza, Ceará.

**Bill No. 3 - 391/2000 (Executive Branch)** - Authorizes the National Institute for Colonization and Land Reform - INCRA - to alienate to the Brazilian Institute of the Environment and Renewable Natural Resources - IBAMA - the property mentioned, and takes other measures.

**Bill No. 4 - 777/2009 (Gorete Pereira)** - Names the Metrofor, in Ceará, as the Fortaleza Metro.

**Bill No. 5 - 063/2009 (Beto Faro)** - Prohibits credit card operators from charging fees for transferring points from customers to other loyalty or reward programs within the scope of the corresponding programs.

## Translation of Brazilian Portuguese Text

**Bill No. 6 - UFO (Federal Senate - Paulo Paim) - Authorizes the Executive Branch to establish the Federal University of the Campaign (UFCAMP) when it is deemed favorable in terms of the respective fiscal burden.**

**Final Session: 24-6-2011**

**Meeting: 1st Session**

**Bill No. 4 - UFO (Mariângela Duarte) - Amends paragraph 2 of Article 46 of Law No. 8,541, of December 23, 1992, which modifies income tax legislation, and adds paragraph 3 to the same article.**

**Final Session: 30-6-2011**

**(and other related bills apposed, numbered 045/2004 to 476/2011)**

**General Context:**

The text comprises a series of bills introduced in the Federal Senate of Brazil, addressing various educational, fiscal, and legal matters.  Key themes include:

* **University Creation:** Bills authorizing the establishment of new universities, such as the Federal Rural University of Vale do Guaporé (UFRVG) and a campus of the Federal University of Ceará (UFC) in Canindé.
* **Fiscal Issues:**  Bills modifying income tax legislation regarding favorable fiscal burdens for certain entities or situations.
* **Education Access:** A bill promoting free pre-university courses in public schools.
* **Legal Amendments:**  Bills amending existing laws, such as those related to income tax and social security benefits.

**Specific Bills:**

* **Bill No. 6 (741/2009):** Authorizes the Executive Branch to establish a campus of the Federal University of Paraná in Nova Tebas, Paraná state.
* **Bill No. 4 (783/2009):** Authorizes the Executive Branch to create an advanced campus of the Federal University of Ceará (UFC) in Canindé, Ceará.
* **Bill No. 3 (463/2004):**  Provides for the possibility of attributing income from work to periods when it is due, if the respective fiscal burden is more favorable.
* **Bill No. 1 (206/2007):** Establishes an income tax exemption for individuals receiving social security and pension benefits.
* **Bill No. 5 (292/2009):**  Allows for the attribution of income from work to periods when it is due, if the respective fiscal burden is more favorable.
* **Bill No. 3 (315/2005):** Authorizes the establishment of the Federal Petroleum Technical School in Cachoeiro de Itapemirim, Espírito Santo state.

From the choice of the 50% formula, the student would receive stipends, naturally, companies and liberal professionals would exclude from the program students from public universities, making them free.

The proposed "stage-scholarships" would be funded by companies or liberal professionals to whom students would provide services as interns. The resources allocated for this type of scholarship would be deductible from the company's gross income for tax purposes.

The attached proposal, authored by Honorable Deputy Eduardo Cunha, allows private higher education institutions to deduct from their income tax the scholarships granted to students who perform voluntary service.

Both bills create new mechanisms for transferring public funds, through tax exemptions, to private higher education institutions. In the main bill, the tax exemption is aimed at businesses and liberal professionals who, by offering internships to students from private higher education institutions, would remunerate interns with resources linked in whole or in part (50%) to the payment of school tuition.

Approved, the companies, liberal professionals, and private higher education institutions would be the beneficiaries. Companies and professionals would be exempted from income tax on resources used for intern compensation. Private institutions would benefit from an increase in the volume of annuities paid by secure sources and the number of enrolled students.

Students, however, would gain and lose in different ways. They would gain from an increase in the number of students with access to higher education. But they would also lose, as internships would become linked to school tuition payments, which currently is not the case.

In fact, internships already exist, regulated by Law No. 6,494 of 1997, linked solely to proper academic formation. Companies and liberal professionals already offer internships to university students to train them in services. The compensation is entirely in kind, and the student uses it as they see fit.

The necessary association between tax incentives, internships, and school tuition payments could encourage the use of interns as "cheap labor," exactly what Law No. 6,954 of 1997 seeks to prevent.

The institutions and students of public higher education would be the losers. Moreover, liberal professionals would also be excluded, as the proposal only contemplates the involvement of private companies and professionals.

Based on the analysis of Law Project No. 3.795/04, it is observed that the matter, despite proposing the deduction of the stage allowance expense from the gross income for income tax purposes and exempting from labor, tax, and social security obligations, does not have budgetary and financial implications. This is because there is no employment relationship between the intern and the company that hired them, provided that the legal requirements are met.

The project does not generate any revenue loss for the Union, as it involves a public policy of providing educational opportunities for students. Therefore, it does not affect the public budget, and no additional measures are required to compensate for the revenue loss.

In accordance with the Internal Norms of the Finance and Taxation Committee, which establishes procedures for examining the budgetary and financial adequacy of proposals, this Committee should approve the project, considering its adequacy in relation to the public finances.

§ 2 If the act of granting or expanding the incentive or benefit referred to in the first paragraph results from the condition mentioned in item II, the benefit will only enter into force when the measures referred to in that item are implemented. (our emphasis)

Law No. 11,768 of August 14, 2008 (Budget Guidelines Law for 2009 - LDO 2009), in Article 93, also reinforces the requirements of the above-quoted provision:

Art. 93. A law or provisional measure that grants or expands an incentive or benefit of a tax nature shall only be approved or issued if it meets the requirements of Article 14 of Complementary Law No. 101 of 2000.

Given this, Technical Note No. 63/2009 of the Brazilian Federal Revenue Service (RFB) estimates the "potential revenue renunciation" of IRPJ in R$ 54 million, R$ 59 million, R$ 65 million, and R$ 71 million for each exercise from 2009 to 2012, respectively.

However, Law Project No. 4.584/04 does not present compensation measures, or at least indicates that the renunciation was considered in the revenue estimate of the budget law, as required by items I and II of Article 14 of the Federal Revenue Law (LRF).

The Project does not offer compensatory measures that would make it fiscally neutral, which is why it cannot be considered adequate and compatible with budgetary and financial requirements.

The Budget Law for the 2009 financial year - LOA/2009, Law No. 11,897 of December 31, 2008, contains an innovative compensation mechanism for budgetary-financial impacts resulting from the issuance of permanent legislation that leads to revenue renunciations resulting from tax benefits or exemptions.

The LOA/2009 program includes, in its work program, a contingency reserve budget unit and a specific credit for the compensation of revenue renunciations, also known as tax revenue or expenditure renunciations, in the following terms:

90.000 – Contingency Reserve – 0999.0E61.0001 – Reserve for Compensation of Renunciations

We note that Law Project No. 4.584/04 was not presented with compensation measures to neutralize the fiscal impact, in accordance with the requirements of Article 14 of Complementary Law No. 101 of 2000.

Preliminarily, it is noted that Project 1/08-CFT is incompatible and inconsistent with Article 61, §1, item II, sub-item “e” of the Federal Constitution. This provision stipulates that any legislative initiative aimed at establishing public administration bodies must be the exclusive prerogative of the President of the Republic.

In this context, Article 8 of the Internal Norms of the Commission of Finance and Taxation, which outlines procedures for assessing the compatibility or adequacy of budgetary and financial matters, states that:

"A proposal that incurs expenses related to the exclusive prerogative of the President of the Republic shall be considered incompatible." (Emphasis added)

Furthermore, the proposal under review, in light of Article 17 of the Law on Fiscal Responsibility (LC 101/2000), binds the entity for a period exceeding two fiscal years, constituting a continuous mandatory expenditure. According to §1 of this article, "acts that create or increase the expenditure referred to in the preceding paragraph must be accompanied by an estimate of the budgetary impact as outlined in item I of Article 16 and demonstrate the source of funds for its financing."

Article 16, item I, specifies:

"Article 16. The creation, expansion, or improvement of government actions that result in an increase in expenditure shall be accompanied by: I - an estimate of the budgetary and financial impact in the exercise in which it is to enter into force and in the two subsequent exercises."

Similarly, Law No. 12,309 of August 9, 2010 (2011 Budget Law) states in Article 91:

"Legislative proposals, in the form of bills, legislative decrees, or provisional measures, that involve or authorize a decrease in revenue or an increase in expenditure for the Union in the 2011 fiscal year must be accompanied by estimates of these effects for each of the exercises covered by the period from 2011 to 2013, detailing the respective calculation and corresponding compensation, in accordance with the constitutional and legal provisions governing the matter."

In line with these provisions, the Commission of Finance and Taxation issued Summary No. 1 in 2008, which considers incompatible and inadequate a proposal, even in an authorizing character, that conflicts with the Law on Fiscal Responsibility by failing to estimate the budgetary and financial impact and demonstrate the source of funds for its financing.

In support of this understanding, the Commission of Finance and Taxation, in its ordinary meeting held on June 15, 2011, concluded unanimously that Project of Law No. 364/2003 (from the Federal Senate) is incompatible and inadequate with budgetary and financial norms due to its failure to present an estimate of its impact and demonstrate the source of funds, as required by Article 4 of Law No. 7,827 of September 27, 1989, which regulates Article 159, item I, sub-item “c”, of the Constitution.

Federal law establishes the Constitutional Funds for:

- Northern Financing (FNO)
- Northeastern Financing (FNE)
- Central-West Financing (FCO),

and takes other provisions; with the opinions of:

- The Economic Development, Industry and Commerce Committee,
- The Amazon, National Integration and Regional Development Committee,
- The Finance and Taxation Committee (Article 54 of the RICD),
- The Constitution and Justice Committee and Citizenship (Article 54 of the RICD).

**Discussion and Approval:**

The proposal is subject to conclusive consideration by the committees (Article 24, II).

**Parental Opinion of the Amazon, National Integration and Regional Development Committee:**

The bill (PL 1,097/2007), originating from the Federal Senate, amends Article 4 of Law No. 7,827, of September 27, 1989, which regulates Article 159, paragraph I, subparagraph "c", of the Federal Constitution, establishing the Constitutional Funds for Northern (FNO), Northeastern (FNE), and Central-West (FCO) Financing, and provides for other measures.

The new text proposed for the opening paragraph of this provision includes the commercial and service sectors of the North, Northeast, and Central-West regions among the productive activities eligible for funding from the respective Constitutional Financing Funds.

The proposal also repeals paragraph 3 of Article 4 of Law No. 7,827/1989 and adds a new paragraph to the same article, stipulating that the limits for financing productive activities as outlined in the opening paragraph of Article 4 shall be defined in the annual financing program referred to in Article 14, paragraph II, of the same law.

Currently, only the agricultural, mining, industrial, and agro-industrial sectors are eligible for funding from these Funds. The proposed changes aim to expand access to financing to other economic sectors in all regions, as outlined in the bill sent by the Federal Senate.

**Conclusion:**

The scope of credit instruments extended to other economic sectors in all regions, which benefit from the Constitutional Financing Funds, as contained in the bill sent by the Federal Senate, should be analyzed, to the extent possible, from the perspective of the legislator when creating the Constitutional Funds. The Federal Constitution of 1988 established in Article 225, §1, III that the public power shall define, in all units of the Federation, territorial spaces and their components to be specially protected, with alterations and suppressions only permitted through law.

With this objective, Law No. 9,985 of July 18, 2000, which establishes the National System of Nature Conservation Units (SNUC), was created.

Article 17 of Law No. 9.985/2000 (SNUC) concerns national forests, considered conservation units for sustainable use. It defines a national forest as an area with predominantly native forest cover, aiming for the multiple sustainable use of forest resources and scientific research, emphasizing sustainable exploration methods of native forests. Its jurisdiction depends on which entity, Union, state, or municipality, is responsible for its creation.

In addition to defining public domain, it establishes a consultative council, aiming for the paritary participation of all societal segments.

Regarding sustainability, the author distinguishes between it and untouchedness. Sustainability seeks to regulate human activities harmoniously, considering three fundamental principles: social welfare, economic factor, and preservation of natural resources. Man is part of the environment and transforms it while respecting these pillars.

Untouchedness, on the other hand, considers natural resources as sacred and unutilizable. From this perspective, man is seen as a threat to this set of goods.

Sustainability, from the viewpoint of productive uses, is represented by a triangle with economic viability, social responsibility, and environmental responsibility as its vertices.

I understand the creation of a Private Natural Heritage Reserve (RPPN) stems from the landowner's meritous intention to preserve private lands. It's crucial to highlight that merely having such an intention doesn't establish an RPPN; on-site presence of a biological diversity (as defined in Article 2, clause III of the National System of Conservation Units - SNUC law) is necessary to justify the creation of a conservation unit.

As a conservation unit, an RPPN is perpetually registered and strictly subject to various procedural and regulatory implications, including normative ones, aimed at preserving and conserving ecosystems, species, and natural habitats within the RPPN.

Constitutional principles guide "lawmaking," establishing limitations on the legislator's actions. In this context, the principle of equality, enshrined in our Constitution, is paramount. It's not enough for the legislator to ensure that the law is clear and objective; they must also guarantee that its application by interpreters is equitable.

Therefore, it's the legislator's responsibility not only to provide equal normative treatment to situations of equality but also to treat situations of inequality unequally. Primarily, they must ensure that this treatment is justified, reasonable, proportional, feasible, and effective.

From this perspective, as a parliamentarian and a citizen, I fully comprehend how the exercise of legislative power directly and indirectly impacts society's positive or negative well-being. Thus, I propose an adjustment to the SNUC law regarding conservation units, aiming to harmonize and standardize equivalent situations currently treated normatively in a context of inequality.

There should be no justification for creating or transforming a conservation unit through a decree, as the public power's ability to establish a unit shouldn't condition its territorial adjustment or transformation.

Lastly, based on legal certainty and in compliance with the constitutional norm, I believe the declassification of a conservation unit should be conducted through a specific law, as it directly impacts the relationships established under its creation in all aspects (environmental, social, and economic), and should only be applied in exceptional cases, after extensive societal debate.

As good opportunities, we argue, lie in the fact that the Ministry of Education is currently implementing an expansive plan for the creation of technical and professional institutions across the entire national territory, which could facilitate the inclusion of the aforementioned locality in the list of beneficiaries of this expansion.

However, the manner in which Senator Artur Virgílio and the Federal Senate intend to move forward with this proposal—through a Legislative Project of an authorizing nature—requires the invocation of the "vicio de iniciativa" (defect of initiative) due to the exclusive constitutional prerogative of the executive branch to establish federal educational institutions, as stipulated in Article 61, Section II, subparagraphs "a" and "e" of the Federal Constitution.

To further curb the progression of projects that may not align with constitutionality, the Commission on Education and Culture issued, in 2001, a "SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS TO REPORTERS" No. 1/2001 - CEC/HOUSE OF DEPUTIES, which was reaffirmed by its members in 2005 and 2007. This document clarifies that, in the case of a project aiming to create educational institutions, "implicating the establishment of public bodies, and, obviously, positions, functions, and employment, as well as resulting in increased expenses," the legislative initiative to create educational institutions "at any level or modality of instruction" is exclusively within the realm of the executive branch. (See Article 61, Section 1, II, of the Federal Constitution).

Thus, according to the Summary, "Legislative Projects of this nature are merely authorizing and, therefore, ineffective, as they do not generate rights or obligations on the part of the public sector, which holds the competence for such prerogatives." It is worth remembering that, from an educational standpoint, the establishment of a public educational institution should be decided in light of an educational plan, an educational policy, or an innovative pedagogical proposal, and so on, where all educational instances, including, of course, schools and their communities, have the right to be heard and to participate. This is the salutary custom in all nations that uphold democratic rule of law.

Therefore, the Report of the Relator on a Legislative Project aimed at establishing a public educational institution should advise against it, as the Ministry of Education already has the power to create such institutions.

In light of the above, I respectfully request that the Ministry of Education be directed to establish the Federal Center for Technological Education in Manacapuru, with its headquarters in the municipality of Manacapuru, in the state of Amazonas.
